Asimov CME Memory Performance

Memory latency and bandwidth of the CME (the Arm C1-SME2 matrix engine unit) on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and boot F2 (prefetchers off). Every measured number is computed from the raw result files when the page is built.

Short version

This page reports how fast the CME (the Arm C1-SME2 matrix engine unit, shared by the two cores of one cluster) loads and stores memory on the Asimov chip, which runs on a hardware emulator, and the tiles under Figure 1 give its read and write rates. With the hardware prefetchers off (boot F2), one chain load (a test load whose value is the address of the next load) takes 21.015 to 21.240 ns for buffers that fit in the L1 cache of the CME and 71.714 ns in the DRAM-model row [Ref1] [Ref2]. These times are 0.010 to 0.235 ns and 50.709 ns above the separate register-only measurement of 21.005 ns (the round-trip baseline), and the differences do not isolate memory-access time.

Boot F1 has the prefetchers on. Its values are in the figure and in the tiles. A prefetcher loads data into a cache before the program asks for it. The DRAM model is an emulator memory model, not silicon timing.

Bandwidth headline numbers: the best rows of three files of each boot. Each row reads or writes the whole buffer in address order. The single-call rows are in cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv [Ref9] [Ref10] and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv [Ref11] [Ref12]. The looped rows are in cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv [Ref13] [Ref14]. F2 is boot F2 (prefetchers off) and F1 is boot F1 (prefetchers on). Single-call form: all passes of a rep (one timed measurement) in one call of the test loop. Looped form: one call per pass. Bracket time: the time between two clock reads in the C program, around the call or calls. 1 GB/s is 1,000,000,000 bytes per second.

1 Words used here

ADD, CMP, SUBS, B.LO, B.NE
The add, compare and branch instructions of the core that step a loop and close it.
address order
A chain kind: each line of the buffer holds the address of the next line. Boot F1 and boot F2 have no row of this kind.
Asimov
The chip under test. One half of it (a hemisphere) runs on a hardware emulator (operator's README).
B/cycle
Bytes per cycle: the rate in GB/s divided by 2.00 cycles per ns. The measured ratio of the core cycle counter to the timer is 1.9994 to 2.0019 cycles per ns.
best rep
The rep whose value the best row repeats. The span time and the counters of a best row come from the first such rep.
best row
The row that the test program itself prints with the label best: the lowest ns per load of a latency footprint, or the highest bracket rate of a bandwidth command.
boot
One start of the emulated chip with one firmware build. All rows of a boot share its firmware settings.
boot F1
The boot with the cluster L3 on and the hardware prefetchers on (operator's README). It has core rows and CME rows. The page writes "boot F1 (prefetchers on)".
boot F2
The boot with the cluster L3 on and the hardware prefetchers off (operator's README). It has CME rows only. The page writes "boot F2 (prefetchers off)".
bracket rate
The bytes moved in a rep divided by its bracket time, in GB/s (CSV column aggregate_GBps).
bracket time
The time between two clock reads in the C program, one before the kernel call or calls and one after.
call-cost rows
The rows of the file cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv. Each one times short kernel calls of the looped form, one call per pass.
chain kind
How the latency test walks its chain: walked many times, walked once, every line flushed first, or address order.
chain load
One load of the latency test. It loads 8 bytes through the CME, and the loaded value is the address of the next load. The instruction LASTB returns that value to the core. Its time is given in ns per load.
chain shape
Which lines of a buffer belong to the chain: every line, or one line per 4 KiB page.
chip time
Time on the clock of the emulated chip. Every time on this page is chip time.
cluster
Two cores that share an L2 cache, an L3 cache, one CME and one port to the mesh. Arm calls it a DSU (DynamIQ Shared Unit).
cluster L3
The level 3 cache that the two cores of a cluster and their CME share.
cluster port
The mesh device through which one cluster sends its requests.
CME
The Arm C1-SME2 matrix engine unit. Each cluster has one, and the two cores of the cluster share it.
CME L1
The level 1 data cache of the CME. Its size is 64 KiB (operator's README).
cme-call row
A latency row that times 64 kernel calls in one bracket, each call directly after the one before it. Each call runs one step of the round-trip baseline.
command
One run of a test program. It is one line of the file log.txt of a boot.
command lifetime
The time from the start to the end of a command. The mesh counters run during that time.
condition number
The ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value of the matrix of a fit. A large value means that the fit cannot separate its coefficients.
control row
A row that is run to check one thing about other rows. Its result is known before the run, or it differs from the row beside it in one item. An example is an L3 hit count of 0 on a boot whose L3 holds no data.
core
One Arm C1-Nano processor. Linux numbers the ten cores CPU 0 to CPU 9. The core rows run the tests with the loads and stores of the core itself, on boot F1 only.
correlation coefficient
The Pearson correlation: a value from -1 to +1 that says how closely two columns follow one straight line. +1 means an exact rising line and -1 an exact falling line.
counting window
The interval between the counter start and the counter stop of one latency row. In the code the counter start comes before the first clock read of the bracket, and the counter stop comes after the second clock read.
crosspoint
One junction of the mesh, named by its position (x,y).
CSV
Comma-separated values: the text format of the result files. One line is one row.
demand-only
Said of a row that counts 0 prefetch refills per load in every pass.
DRAM model
The memory behind the mesh on this emulator. It is an emulator memory model, not silicon DRAM timing.
DSB ST
A barrier instruction that waits until the stores before it are complete.
DSB SY
A barrier instruction that waits until all memory accesses before it are complete.
DSU 1
The cluster of CPUs 2 and 3. Its CME runs every CME row of this page, called from CPU 2.
DUP
An instruction that copies a register of the core into a vector.
effective cycles per 64 bytes transferred
64 divided by the rate in B/cycle: the cycles of a whole loop divided by the number of 64-byte units that the loop transfers. It is a loop throughput. It is not the time that one load or one store takes to complete.
effective rate
A loop throughput: what a whole rep transfers, divided by the time of the rep. It is not the time that one load or one store takes to complete.
EOR
The instruction for the XOR operation.
est.
Marks an estimate: a value derived with an assumption, not read from a row.
every line flushed first
A chain kind. It is "walked once" with one more step: the core removes every line of the buffer from the caches before each timed rep.
excess
The requests received by the home node of the region minus the level subtracted.
fold
The XOR of all loaded 8-byte words into one value. The read kernels return it to the core.
footprint
The size of the buffer that a test walks. A copy uses two buffers of that size.
free intercept
A constant term of a fit whose value the fit chooses.
GB/s
Gigabytes per second, with 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes. 1 GB/s equals 1 byte per ns.
hit share
The L3 hit count divided by the sum of the L3 hit count and the L3 miss count of one row.
home node
A mesh device that owns a range of addresses. Each of the five home nodes holds one part of the SLC and one OCM region.
idle control
A mesh count taken while a small command runs that sends almost no requests to the home nodes. It gives the background count.
in flight
A line request is in flight between the moment the CME sends it and the moment the line arrives.
inner refill
A CME L1 refill whose line came from inside the cluster (event 0x327D): from the cluster L3 or from a snoop of a core's cache (operator's README). It counts loads and prefetches alike.
intercept
The time that a fitted straight line gives at 0 bytes per pass.
ISB
An instruction that makes the core finish the instructions in flight before the next one starts.
kernel
One test loop written in assembly in the file cme_kern.S. On this page the word never means the Linux kernel.
KiB, MiB
1,024 bytes and 1,024 KiB.
L3 events
Three CME events: 0x328E (L3 hit), 0x328F (L3 miss) and 0x3290 (L3 refill). They are exploratory: no control row validates them.
L3 hit count
Event 0x328E (CME_L3D_CACHE_HIT) per chain load. Exploratory.
L3 miss count
Event 0x328F (CME_L3D_CACHE_MISS) per chain load. Exploratory.
L3 refill count
Event 0x3290 (CME_L3D_CACHE_REFILL) per chain load. Exploratory.
L3-event rows
The rows of the latency test that count the three L3 events of the CME.
LASTB
An instruction that copies the last active element of a vector to a register of the core.
latency test
The loop of chain loads over a chain of 64-byte lines in random order. Its result is the time per chain load in ns.
LD1D, LD1B
Vector load instructions. LD1D loads 8-byte elements, LD1B loads bytes.
LDP, STP
The core instructions that load or store a pair of registers.
least-squares fit
The coefficients that make the sum of the squared residuals smallest.
level subtracted
The background count that is taken off the count of a home node. In a command on one region it is the mean count of the four home nodes that do not hold the region.
LLVM model
The scheduling description of the C1-Nano in the LLVM compiler source.
load pipe, store pipe
Execution units of the CME in the LLVM model. The load pipe runs the vector loads one after the other. The store pipe does the same for the vector stores.
lone call
A kernel call that stands alone in its bracket: the bracket holds this one call.
looped form
The bandwidth test with one kernel call per pass.
mesh
The on-chip network (Arm CMN) that joins the clusters, the home nodes and the bridges to memory. It is a grid of 6 x 6 crosspoints.
mesh counters
Counters of the mesh. They count the requests that each home node receives during one whole command.
mesh step
A move from one crosspoint to the next one. The step count between two crosspoints is the difference in x plus the difference in y.
miss minus refill
The L3 miss count minus the L3 refill count of one row.
OCM
On-chip memory: cache ways of the home nodes that the firmware locks and maps as memory. Five regions of 256 KiB, one in each home node.
outer refill
A CME L1 refill whose line came from outside the cluster, through the mesh (event 0x327E). It counts loads and prefetches alike.
outside-span time
Bracket time minus span time. It holds the C call and return, the register save and restore, SMSTART, SMSTOP and the bookkeeping of the second stamp.
pass
One walk over the whole buffer or the whole chain.
plain rows
The rows of the latency test at the same footprints with the refill counters and no L3 event.
plan rule
The fit rule of the run plan for a straight line of time per pass against bytes per pass. A largest residual over 2 % of the smallest pass time makes the intercept void. The page then quotes neither the intercept nor the rate of that fit.
PMU
Performance monitoring unit: the event counters of the core.
prefetch refill
A CME L1 refill that the hardware prefetcher of the CME asked for, not a load of the program (event 0x32B2).
prefetcher
Hardware that requests lines before the program loads them. The cores and the CME each have one. They are on in boot F1 and off in boot F2 (operator's README).
read refill
A CME L1 refill caused by a load of the program that missed (event 0x3280).
refill
The arrival of one 64-byte line in the CME L1 after a miss or a prefetch.
rep
One timed measurement. It is one data row of a CSV file and can hold many passes. In the rows that walk a chain once, one rep is one pass.
rep spread
The highest value minus the lowest value over the reps (or timed passes) of one row. The page gives it in the unit of the value, or in percent of the lowest value, and says which.
repeat difference
The difference between two measurements of the same row inside one boot, in percent of the lower value.
requests received
The mesh counter event hns_pocq_reqs_recvd_all of one home node: the number of requests that the node received while the command ran.
residual
The measured value of a row minus the value that a fit gives for the same row.
rms
Root mean square: the square root of the mean of the squared residuals of a fit.
round-trip baseline
The row cme-roundtrip: the loop of the latency test with a register copy (DUP) in place of the load. A value goes from the core to the CME and back, and no memory is accessed. It is a separate measurement. A chain load minus this value is the measured difference between two kernels, not a memory-access time.
RTL
Register transfer level: the source text of the hardware design.
run plan
The project file follow-up-run-plan.md. Its section 13 plans the rows that measure the cost of a kernel call, and it holds the fit rule.
SHA-256 checksum
A 256-bit value computed from the bytes of a file. Two files with the same checksum have the same content.
single-call form
The bandwidth test with all passes of a rep inside one kernel call.
SLC
System level cache: the cache inside the mesh, held by the five home nodes. 3.75 MiB est. after the OCM ways are taken out (operator's README).
SMSTART, SMSTOP
The instructions that enter and leave streaming mode.
snoop
A request to another cache of the cluster for a line that it holds.
span rate
The bytes moved in a rep divided by its span time, in GB/s (CSV column span_GBps).
span time
The time between the two stamps of a kernel call. The first stamp follows SMSTART. The second stamp comes before SMSTOP.
ST1B
A vector store instruction.
stamp
One read of the timer register inside a kernel. Each kernel call takes two stamps, and the time between them is the span time.
streaming mode
The processor state between the instructions SMSTART and SMSTOP. In it, vector loads and stores run on the CME.
test plan
The project file CME-plan.md: the design of the CME load and store test.
TF-A
Trusted Firmware-A: the firmware stage that sets the prefetcher controls before Linux starts (operator's README).
thread barrier
The point where the worker thread of the test program waits for the main thread before each rep.
TLB
Translation lookaside buffer: the cache of address translations.
vector
One CME register of 64 bytes. One vector load or store moves 64 bytes, which is one cache line.
walked many times
A chain kind: one chain is walked again and again inside a rep, until at least 65,536 loads are done.
walked once
A chain kind: two untimed walks of a first chain touch the lines. Each timed rep then walks another chain over the same lines one time.
warm-up pass
One untimed pass over the buffer before each rep of the bandwidth test.
write refill
A CME L1 refill caused by a store of the program that missed (event 0x3281).
XOR
The bitwise exclusive-or operation (instruction EOR).
ZA array
The matrix register of SME, the Arm Scalable Matrix Extension.

2 What was measured

Key points
  • The page uses two boots of one emulated chip. Boot F1 (prefetchers on) and boot F2 (prefetchers off) ran the same 70 CME commands on CPU 2.
  • Two tests produce every CME row. The latency test gives the time per chain load. The bandwidth test gives the bytes per time when the CME reads, writes or copies a whole buffer in address order.
  • Each row has a bracket time and a span time. Both come from a timer of 1 ns steps. Both cycle counters read 2.000 cycles per ns.
  • All files that the checksum lists name match their checksums. No command failed.

2.1 The platform and the path of one CME load

  • A CME load that misses the CME L1 cache gets its line from one of two places. One is inside the cluster. The other is outside it, through the mesh: a home node or the DRAM model.
  • The raw files show only part of this path. The tag on each box of Figure 2 names the source of the fact in the box.

The DRAM model is an emulator memory model. No DRAM latency or bandwidth number on this page is silicon DRAM timing [Ref20].

Insufficient data

The Arm C1-SME2 manual is not on disk. So the size of the CME L1 cache is not confirmed from the document itself [Ref19]. The Linux cache listing prints ways=0 for every level. So the folders do not give the number of ways of any cache [Ref15]. A copy of the manual and a read of the cache geometry registers would resolve both.

2.2 The two boots

  • Both boots ran the same 70 CME command lines in the same order on CPU 2, with the cluster L3 on [Ref22] [Ref23].
  • The intended difference is the firmware setting of the hardware prefetchers [Ref21].
  • The counters agree with the setting. The CME L1 refills caused by the prefetcher read 0.0553 to 16.1819 per load on boot F1 and 0.0000 per load on boot F2, in all 104 chain rep rows of each boot. A value above 1 means that the row counts more prefetch refills than loads.
  • Section 4.3 draws the prefetch refills per load against the footprint for both boots [Ref1] [Ref3] [Ref5] [Ref6].

Note

A difference between a boot F1 row and a boot F2 row is a difference between two boots. The prefetcher setting is one difference. Two more are known. Boot F1 ran its self-test and 67 core commands before the CME commands, and boot F2 ran the CME commands alone. Each command draws its own physical pages. So the buffers of a row need not sit on the same pages on the two boots [Ref21].

Sign of a difference

How the page compares the two boots: a difference in ns is boot F1 minus boot F2. A ratio names its two boots in the column header or in the sentence, for example "F2 / F1" or "boot F1 is 2 times boot F2".

Insufficient data

Each setting was booted once. The boot-to-boot spread of a row is unknown. A second boot with the same settings would give it.

2.3 The latency test and the round-trip baseline

  • One chain load is two instructions on the CME. LD1D loads 8 bytes. LASTB moves them to the core as the address of the next load [Ref28]. So each load waits for the load before it. The time per load is the time from the start of one load to the start of the next.
  • The round-trip baseline runs the same loop with a register copy in place of the load. It reads 21.005 ns in all 24 CME latency files of the two boots [Ref25]. It is a separate measurement with no memory access.
  • Both loops return a value to the core through LASTB [Ref28]. The rows do not show that the instructions which the two loops share cost the same time in both.

A rep is one timed measurement, and a pass is one walk over the whole chain. The reps are counted per footprint. In the kind "walked many times" one rep is many passes. In the other kinds one rep is one pass. Counts are from the rows of boot F2. The address-order kind (each line points to the next line) was not run on these boots.

  • A chain is one random cycle through all its lines. The seeds are fixed. So both boots walk the same chains [Ref29].
  • The core writes the buffer and the chain pointers. Then the CME walks the first chain twice, untimed, before the first rep [Ref29].
  • Each latency file also holds cme-call rows: 64 calls of the baseline kernel with one step each, timed in one bracket. Their best rows read 124.516 to 125.609 ns per call over the 24 files [Ref25]. Section 7.5 uses them.
  • No row gives a CME load time without the return to the core. Every latency kernel returns the loaded value to the core through LASTB.
  • The page gives "chain load minus round-trip baseline" as the measured difference between two kernels: the chain-load kernel and the baseline kernel [Ref28].
Insufficient data

The rows do not show how much of a chain load time is memory-access time. The chain-load kernel runs LD1D and then LASTB. The baseline kernel runs DUP and then LASTB [Ref28]. No row measures the time that the two kernels share outside the memory access. A calibration of that shared time would resolve it, for example a waveform of one iteration of each kernel. The project file README.md states the same limit: the chain load minus the baseline is a derived number, not the memory latency [Ref30].

2.4 The bandwidth test and the kernels

  • A bandwidth row is the bytes moved in a rep divided by the time.
  • The CSV files use 5 kernel names. A kernel name can stand for several forms: looped, single-call, looped without the final fold, and looped with a DSB ST barrier. Figure 4 and Table 4 define them. The CSV row does not name its form. The file name and the header comment of the command do [Ref31].
  • A read row measures the loads together with the XOR work of the fold. It is not the rate of the loads alone [Ref28].

The names cme-ldr16 and cme-str16 come from the options of the core test. Through the CME they move 64 bytes per instruction. The 74 bandwidth best rows of a boot include the 7 OCM rows.

  • A rep runs in this order: one untimed pass in the looped form (also for a single-call rep), a flush of every line when the command asks for it, a wait at a thread barrier, a clock read, the kernel call or calls, a clock read [Ref32].
  • A buffer over all five OCM regions is five segments. One looped pass over it is five kernel calls, one per region [Ref32].
  • The fold is not printed. A separate self-test checks the folds. It ran on boot F1 with 0 failures and did not run on boot F2 (operator's README) [Ref20].
  • The bandwidth rows carry no counters. The program refuses its counter option together with the CME option [Ref32].
Insufficient data

The files do not show whether the ISB that closes a span waits for the loads or stores of the span to complete. A waveform of one call, or a statement by Arm on ISB and CME operations in flight, would resolve it [Ref28].

2.5 Bracket time, span time and the best row

  • Every CME row carries two times. The bracket time runs between two clock reads in C around the kernel call or calls. The span time runs between two stamps (timer reads inside the kernel), after SMSTART and before SMSTOP [Ref28] [Ref33].
  • The outside-span time is the bracket time minus the span time. Figure 4 shows what each time covers. The wall-clock lanes figure in section 7.1 draws the two times of one call to scale.

Table 5. The two times of a row [Ref28] [Ref33].

Bracket timeSpan time
Clockclock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC), read in Cthe timer register CNTVCT_EL0, read in the kernel
Startsbefore the C call of the kernelafter SMSTART and an ISB
Endsafter the kernel returnsafter the loop, the fold or the DSB ST, and an ISB. Before SMSTOP.
Holdsthe span, and also the call and the return, the save and restore of registers, SMSTART, SMSTOP, and the C loop around the calls of the looped formthe setup of the kernel, the loop, the fold or the DSB ST, and the closing ISB
Latency CSV columnns_per_loadns_per_load_span
Bandwidth CSV columnaggregate_GBps (bytes / bracket time)span_GBps (bytes / sum of the spans of the rep)

The outside-span time is not the cost of the mode switch alone. It holds every item of the bracket column that the span column lacks.

  • On the footprint rows of the latency test the two times are close. Bracket minus span is 0.001 to 0.038 ns per load on boot F1 and 0.000 to 0.041 ns per load on boot F2. Rows: the 58 chain rep rows of cme-latency-dram-small.csv and cme-latency-dram-large.csv of each boot [Ref1] [Ref3] [Ref5] [Ref6]. One kernel call covers thousands of loads there.
  • The two clock reads of an empty bracket cost 39.0 ns (boot F1) and 39.0 to 40.0 ns (boot F2). Each CME latency file prints this value in a comment line [Ref25].
  • Which row the page quotes:
    • Latency: the best row is the lowest bracket ns per load over the reps of a footprint [Ref29].
    • Bandwidth: the best row is the rep with the highest bracket GB/s. Its span rate is the span rate of that same rep [Ref32].
    • A latency best row prints no span time and no counters. The page takes them from the first rep row whose bracket ns per load equals the best row.
    • The files hold 234 latency rep rows and 270 bandwidth rep rows per boot. The page states it when it uses rep rows and not best rows.

2.6 The counters

  • Each latency rep row carries the core cycle counter and six CME events, read through the PMU of the core [Ref33].
  • In the 10 files without -l3 in the name, five of the six events count CME L1 refills: three by cause and two by source. In the 2 files with -l3 in the name the three cause events give way to the three L3 events [Ref25].
  • The two groups count the same refills in these rows: cause and source differ by at most 0.00002 per load on boot F2 and 0.00030 per load on boot F1, over 104 rep rows of each boot [Ref25].

Counts per load are the count of the window divided by the loads of the row.

  • In the order of the code the counter start comes before the first clock read of the bracket, and the counter stop comes after the second clock read. So the counting window holds the bracket, the two clock reads and the return from the system call that starts the counters. The flush runs before the window [Ref29].
  • Every count of a row is a total over its window. The rows hold no time stamp of a counter start or stop.
  • The mesh counters cover the whole life of a command: the fill of the buffer, the untimed passes, the flushes and the reps together. 15 of the 70 CME commands of each boot ran under them [Ref34].
  • The bandwidth rows carry no counter of the core or of the CME.
Insufficient data

The three L3 events (0x328E, 0x328F, 0x3290) have no independent check of their hit and miss meaning [Ref33] [Ref38] [Ref39]. A boot whose L3 holds no data, where the hit event must read 0, would be one necessary check. The page reports these columns as counts. Every reading of a count as the level that served a load is inside a block labelled Hypothesis.

Insufficient data

The project file README.md describes the two mesh sums in one line each [Ref30]. hns_mc_reqs_local_all is the number of requests that all home nodes sent on to memory. hns_cache_miss_all is the miss count of the SLC over all nodes. Their exact definitions are not in the folders. The event table of the Arm CMN manual would give them.

2.7 The clock

  • The timer behind both times ticks at 1,000,000,000 Hz. One tick is 1 ns.
  • The header of every CME command prints this frequency [Ref25] [Ref31], and the Linux boot log of both boots prints it too [Ref16] [Ref17].
  • The cycle counter of the core and the cycle counter of the CME both read 2.000 cycles per ns. This is a measurement: the counted cycles of a row divided by its time [Ref25].

Table 7. Cycles per ns, exact values [Ref25].

BootCounterRatioRep rowsLowestMedianHighest

Boot F1 (prefetchers on)Core cycle countercycles / bracket ns1561.99992.00012.0019
Boot F2 (prefetchers off)CME cycle counter (0x3246)CME cycles / span ns1561.99952.00012.0009
Boot F1 (prefetchers on)CME cycle counter (0x3246)CME cycles / span ns1562.00002.00012.0007
  • Example: one step of the round-trip baseline reads 21.005 to 21.006 ns and 42.01 to 42.02 core cycles in the rep rows of both boots [Ref25].
  • On short rows the core cycle counter reads above 2.0 cycles per bracket ns: 2.05 to 2.14 on passes of 64 loads, 2.01 to 2.03 on passes of 320 loads and 2.02 to 2.04 on the cme-call rows (both boots) [Ref25].
  • In the order of the code the counting window starts before the bracket and ends after it. So it counts cycles that the bracket time does not hold [Ref29]. Section 7.7 gives the core cycle count as time minus the bracket time. The rows hold no time stamp that places that difference before or after the bracket.
  • For time on those rows the page uses the ns columns, not the cycle columns. Section 7.7 also covers the CME cycle counter on the cme-call rows.
  • The Linux boot log also prints "2000.00 BogoMIPS" (a speed value that Linux prints at boot). Linux computes it from the timer frequency. So it is not evidence of the core clock [Ref16].
  • All times are chip time on the emulator. The real time on the emulator host is much longer and is in no CSV file.

2.8 Data integrity

  • Every file listed in the checksum list of each run folder matches its SHA-256 checksum: 88 of 88 on boot F1 and 30 of 30 on boot F2. The page generator computes the checksums when it builds the page [Ref26] [Ref27].
  • The lists cover every result file and the Linux boot log. They do not cover README.md and SHA256SUMS.
  • README.md is the operator's README, the source of every fact with that tag on this page. It has no checksum.
  • No command failed [Ref22] [Ref23].
  • In every counter row the counter group ran for the whole time it was enabled [Ref25].

3 Results at a glance

Key points
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off), a chain load takes 21.015 to 21.240 ns for buffers that fit in the CME L1 and 71.714 ns in the DRAM-model row.
  • The round-trip baseline is 21.005 ns in all 24 files. It is a separate measurement with no memory access.
  • The chain loads are 0.010 to 0.235 ns (CME L1) and 50.709 ns (DRAM model) above the baseline. Each number is the measured difference between two kernels. It does not isolate the time of the memory access.
  • A single-call read inside the CME L1 runs at 110.8 to 132.4 GB/s on boot F2 (prefetchers off). A single-call write runs at 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s on both boots.
  • No boot was repeated. Every repeat difference of this section is a difference inside one boot.

3.1 What a chain load costs, by where the line comes from

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the chain load is 21.015 to 21.240 ns (CME L1), 32.779 ns (inside the cluster), 42.125 to 43.666 ns (outside the cluster), 45.546 ns (OCM) and 71.714 ns (DRAM model).
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) every row counts prefetch refills, at least 0.0553 per load. So a boot F1 value is not the cost of one cache level.

Best row of each footprint. Span time and counters come from the first rep that equals the best row. "Chain load minus the baseline" is the bracket time of the chain-load kernel minus the bracket time of the round-trip kernel, which is 21.005 ns. It is the measured difference between two kernels [Ref28]. It is not a measured part of a chain load, and it is not the time of the memory access. The cycles column is that difference multiplied by the measured 2.00 cycles per ns (section 2.7). "F1 minus F2" is the F1 bracket time minus the F2 bracket time, the bold number of the figure. On boot F2 every row counts 0.00 prefetch refills per load.

What the table shows on boot F2 (prefetchers off):

  • An OCM load takes 1.880 to 3.421 ns more than the 1 MiB and 3 MiB rows.
  • An OCM load takes 26.168 ns less than the DRAM model row with every line flushed first.
  • The 32 MiB row walked once (71.068 ns) is within 0.646 ns of the DRAM model row (71.714 ns). It counts 0.9953 outer refills per load. No counter says how many of them the SLC serves (section 9.9).

Limits of this comparison:

  • The rows do not share one setup.
    • The OCM row uses 4 KiB pages and a flush before the walk [Ref17].
    • The outside-the-cluster rows of 1 MiB and 3 MiB carry backing=hugetlb and flush=0 in the file of boot F2 [Ref3]. So they use huge pages and no flush.
    • The huge page size is 2 MiB. It is read on boot F1, the one boot that wrote a system listing [Ref15].
  • The outside-the-cluster rows count 0.8134 and 0.9311 outer refills per load, not 1.0000. The same rows count 0.1866 and 0.0689 inner refills per load. These counts are totals of a rep.
  • The round-trip baseline is a separate measurement.
    • Every chain load returns its result to the core through the instruction LASTB [Ref28].
    • The round-trip kernel runs a register copy in place of the load, then the same LASTB.
    • No row measures the time that the two kernels share.
    • So a chain load minus the baseline is a difference between two kernels. No row gives the time of the memory access alone.
  • The DRAM model has no configured delay (operator's README) [Ref20]. Its time is the delay of the emulated path, not the timing of a memory part.
  • The inside-the-cluster row counts 0.9970 inner refills per load. An inner refill comes from the cluster L3 or from a snoop of a core's cache (operator's README) [Ref21]. The counters of this file do not separate the two.
Insufficient data

The memory-access time of a chain load is unknown. The rows give the chain load (21.015 to 21.240 ns in the CME L1 rows of boot F2 (prefetchers off)) and the separate round-trip baseline (21.005 ns). A calibration of the non-memory time that the chain-load kernel and the round-trip kernel share would resolve it. With it, the difference of 0.010 to 0.235 ns could be read as memory-access time.

3.2 Numbers to quote

  • For latency, quote the boot F2 (prefetchers off) rows. Every rep of these rows counts 0.0000 prefetch refills per load. So no prefetched line shortens a chain load.
  • For bandwidth, quote the single-call form inside the CME L1 and the looped form above it.
  • State the boot with every read rate above the CME L1. At 96 KiB the looped read is 43.7 GB/s on boot F1 and 40.0 GB/s on boot F2. At 32 MiB it is 36.6 GB/s and 17.7 GB/s.

No counter of these files says where a stored line goes.

3.3 Measured rates against the documented limits

  • The single-call read transfers 55.4 to 66.2 B/cycle on boot F2 (prefetchers off). That is an effective rate of 0.87 to 1.03 vectors of 64 B per cycle.
  • One load instruction of the read kernel loads 4 vectors [Ref28]. So the effective rate is 0.22 to 0.26 load instructions per cycle on boot F2 (prefetchers off). The documented limit is 2 load or store instructions per cycle [Ref18].
  • The single-call write transfers 25.8 to 26.7 B/cycle on boot F2 (prefetchers off). That is an effective 2.40 to 2.48 cycles per 64 B transferred.
  • Every measured number of this subsection is a throughput.
    • It divides the bracket time of a whole rep by the bytes that the rep transfers.
    • One iteration of the read loop runs 4 load instructions of 4 vectors each and 16 EOR instructions (bitwise exclusive-or) [Ref28].
    • One iteration of the write loop runs 4 store instructions of 4 vectors each [Ref28].
    • So no measured number of this subsection is the time that one load or one store takes to complete.

A range covers the 5 footprints. One iteration of the read loop reads 1 KiB with 23 instructions, 4 of them load instructions [Ref28]. Cycles are core cycles at 2.00 cycles per ns. An effective value is the bracket time of a whole rep divided by what the rep transfers. It is not the time that one load or one store takes to complete.

The documented limits:

  • The core issues at most 2 load or store instructions per cycle to the CME (Arm Software Optimization Guide) [Ref18]. The guide gives no limit in vectors or in bytes.
  • The LLVM model of the core has 1 CME load pipe and 1 CME store pipe [Ref42].
  • The LLVM model holds the CME load pipe for 2 cycles for one load of 4 vectors [Ref42]. That is 2 vectors per cycle, or 128 B/cycle (est.).
Hypothesis

The load path of the CME limits the read rate. The EOR work does not. The measured read rate is 43 to 52 % of the 128 B/cycle of the LLVM model (est.). The read kernel also runs one EOR instruction for every loaded vector. So these rows cannot separate the load path from the EOR work.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A read kernel with no EOR instruction in its loop, run at the same footprints. A rate that stays at the measured value confirms it. A higher rate rejects it.

Insufficient data

No row explains why the single-call write transfers 64 B in an effective 2.38 to 2.49 cycles. A write kernel under a counter of the CME store pipe, or a waveform of one write pass, would show where the cycles go.

How to read a difference on this page:

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the plain row and the L3-event row of each latency footprint agree within 0.92 % at all 23 footprints (4 KiB to 32 MiB). A difference below 1 % between two such rows is not larger than the largest repeat difference of these rows.
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on), 3 of 23 footprints differ by more than 1.0 % (8 KiB, 16 KiB and 192 KiB).
  • A looped rate inside the CME L1 differs by 0.19 to 11.22 % (bracket rate) and by 0.38 to 12.15 % (span rate) between two files of one boot. A difference below 12.2 % between two looped rates inside the CME L1 is not larger than the largest repeat difference of these rows.
Hypothesis

The prefetcher makes the reps of boot F1 (prefetchers on) differ more at 8 KiB, 16 KiB and 192 KiB.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: More reps of these footprints with the prefetch refill counter beside the time. The L3-event rows do not carry that counter. Section 5.7 holds the rep values and the inner plus outer refills of each rep. A count that follows the time confirms it. A count that does not follow the time rejects it.

Insufficient data

The boot-to-boot spread is unknown. No boot was repeated. A second boot with the settings of boot F1, and one with the settings of boot F2, would give it. Until then, no row separates the effect of the prefetchers from the boot-to-boot spread and from the other differences between the two boots (section 9.8).

4 Latency by footprint

Key points
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the chain load takes these times:
    • 4 KiB to 64 KiB: 21.015 to 21.240 ns.
    • 96 KiB to 384 KiB: 32.779 to 35.979 ns.
    • 1 MiB to 3 MiB: 42.125 to 43.666 ns.
    • 16 MiB to 32 MiB: 69.254 to 71.068 ns.
  • The round-trip baseline is a separate measurement with no memory access. It is 21.005 ns per step on both boots.
  • The rows that fit the CME L1 read 0.010 to 0.235 ns above it. This is a measured difference between two kernels. It is not a memory-access time (section 4.2).
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) the same test is slower at every footprint from 4 KiB to 8 MiB, by 0.474 to 24.270 ns. The CME counts up to 15.89 prefetch refills per load there (48 KiB).

4.1 Chain load against footprint

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the chain load stays inside a narrow band in three footprint ranges:
    • 4 KiB to 64 KiB: within 0.225 ns.
    • 96 KiB to 384 KiB: within 3.200 ns.
    • 1 MiB to 3 MiB: within 1.541 ns.
  • From 4 MiB to 32 MiB it rises by 23.740 ns.
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) every row is above the baseline. The lowest row (4 KiB) is 0.484 ns above it.
  • The boot F1 (prefetchers on) curve rises to 53.806 ns at 384 KiB. It reads 43.212 ns at 512 KiB. It rises again to 70.482 ns at 32 MiB.

"Minus baseline" is the chain load minus the round-trip baseline of 21.005 ns. It is a measured difference between two kernels (section 4.2). The core has no such baseline.

How to read the rows:

  • The latency test builds a chain over a buffer. The footprint is the size of that buffer.
  • A CME chain load is one vector load (LD1D) and one move of the value back to a core register (LASTB).
  • Rows up to 384 KiB are walked many times. Rows from 512 KiB are walked once [Ref29].
  • Each footprint has 3 timed measurements when it is walked many times and 2 when it is walked once. Each one is a rep.
  • The table quotes the bracket time of the best rep.
  • The span time of the same rep is 0.000 to 0.041 ns per load lower on boot F2 (prefetchers off), over all rep rows.
  • It is 0.001 to 0.038 ns per load lower on boot F1 (prefetchers on).
  • The largest step on boot F2 (prefetchers off) is between 64 KiB and 96 KiB: +14.739 ns.
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the chain load still rises by 1.814 ns from 16 MiB to 32 MiB. So the curve is not flat at its last point.

4.2 Chain load minus the round-trip baseline

  • The round-trip baseline reads 21.005 ns per step in all 24 CME latency files of the two boots. It is 42.01 to 42.02 core cycles per step.
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the chain load is 0.010 to 0.235 ns above the baseline at 4 KiB to 64 KiB.
  • It is 11.774 to 14.974 ns above the baseline at 96 KiB to 384 KiB.
  • The chain load and the baseline are two kernels [Ref28]. A kernel is one test loop in cme_kern.S.
  • A step of the chain kernel is a load (LD1D) and a move of the value back to the core (LASTB).
  • A step of the baseline kernel is a register copy (DUP) and the same move (LASTB). It reads no memory.
  • Every refill counter reads zero in every rep of the baseline.
  • The cycle columns of the baseline do not read zero. They read 42.01 to 42.02 core cycles and 42.0039 to 42.0068 CME cycles per step.
  • So "chain load minus baseline" is a measured difference between two kernels. It is the time of a step with a load minus the time of a step with a register copy.
  • The rows do not show that the two kernels share one fixed cost per step. So the rows do not show that the chain load contains the baseline time, or that the difference is the time of the memory access.
  • The core in its own L1 takes 2.002 to 2.117 ns per load (4 KiB to 32 KiB, boot F1).
  • The CME chain load in its own L1 reads 0.010 to 0.235 ns above the baseline (4 KiB to 64 KiB, boot F2).
  • The blue line is above the aqua line only from 96 KiB to 384 KiB, by 1.023 to 9.152 ns.
  • At 768 KiB the blue line is 0.046 ns below the aqua line. That is less than the rep spread of that row (0.289 ns).
  • This comparison crosses two boots. The core rows are from boot F1, with the prefetchers on.
  • On boot F1 alone, the CME chain load is 18.201 to 43.254 ns above the core at every footprint from 4 KiB to 32 MiB.
  • With every line flushed first (8 MiB) the CME on boot F1 is 9.422 ns above the core.
Insufficient data

Whether "chain load minus baseline" is the time of the memory access. The two boots have no row that measures the cost that the two kernels share outside the memory access. A calibration of that shared cost would be needed to read the difference as memory-access time. A kernel with a chain of loads that stays in the CME registers would give the load time without the move to the core.

Insufficient data

Boot F2 has no core rows. A core latency run on a boot with the prefetchers off would give the core against the CME on one boot without prefetch.

4.3 Refill counters per load at each footprint

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the refill counts per load differ by footprint group:
    • 4 KiB to 64 KiB: the rows count at most 0.0156 refills per load.
    • 96 KiB to 384 KiB: the rows count 0.9522 to 1.0000 inner refills per load.
    • 512 KiB and 768 KiB: the rows count refills of both sources, with 0.4229 and 0.7075 outer refills per load.
    • 1 MiB to 32 MiB: the rows count 0.8134 to 0.9953 outer refills per load.
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) the CME refills its L1 4.16 to 16.66 times per load from 8 KiB to 384 KiB.
  • 3.99 to 15.89 of these refills per load are prefetch refills.

Boot F2 (prefetchers off), by rows:

  • 4 KiB to 64 KiB: the rows count 0.0010 to 0.0156 inner refills per load and at most 0.00002 outer refills per load. The CME L1 holds 64 KiB (operator's README) [Ref20]. So these footprints fit in it.
  • 96 KiB to 384 KiB: the rows count 0.9876 to 1.0000 read refills per load. Of these, 0.9522 to 1.0000 per load are inner and 0.0000 to 0.0478 per load are outer. So the inner counter counts most refills of these rows.
    • The inner counter does not say which cache inside the cluster.
    • It can be the cluster L3, which holds 256 KiB [Ref15].
    • It can also be a snoop of a core's cache (operator's README) [Ref20].
    • Section 5 (The cluster L3 as seen by the CME) reads the L3 events of these footprints.
  • 512 KiB and 768 KiB: the outer refills are 0.4229 and 0.7075 per load. The inner refills are 0.5771 and 0.2925 per load. So these two rows count refills of both sources.
  • 1 MiB to 3 MiB: the rows count 0.8134 to 0.9311 outer refills per load. So the outer counter counts most refills of these rows. The chain load stays within 1.541 ns over the group.
  • 4 MiB to 8 MiB: the chain load rises from 47.328 ns to 62.826 ns with 0.9457 to 0.9683 outer refills per load.
  • 16 MiB and 32 MiB: the outer refills are 0.9878 and 0.9953 per load.
  • Every count of this list is a total of a rep. A total does not say which load caused which refill.
Hypothesis

The SLC supplies the outer refills from 1 MiB to 3 MiB (0.8134 to 0.9311 per load). Its size is 3.75 MiB est.: 5 MiB in five home nodes, with 4 of 16 ways of each node locked as OCM (operator's README) [Ref20]. The CME counters say only "outside the cluster". In support, the chain load stays within 1.541 ns from 1 MiB to 3 MiB and reads 3.662 ns more at 4 MiB.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A walked-once row of 1 MiB to 3 MiB under the mesh counters. Requests that the home nodes answer without a cache miss would confirm it. Requests that the home nodes pass on to the DRAM model would reject it.

Observations on the 96 KiB to 384 KiB rows of boot F2 (prefetchers off) [Ref1]:

  • From 96 KiB to 192 KiB the chain load falls as the footprint grows: 35.979, 35.633, 33.910 ns.
  • The read, inner and outer counters of these best reps differ by at most 0.0147 per load. They do not explain the fall.
  • Insufficient data: no validated counter names the source of these inner refills. Section 5.2 gives the exploratory L3 event counts of the same footprints, and section 9.6 gives one hypothesis with its test.
  • The 256 KiB row reads 32.779 ns. Its rep spread is 2.154 ns. That is more than its distance of 1.131 ns to the 192 KiB row.
  • At 256 KiB the 3 reps read 34.933, 33.988, 32.779 ns and count 0.1082, 0.0871, 0.0030 outer refills per load. The rep with the fewest outer refills is the fastest.

Boot F1 (prefetchers on), by rows [Ref5] [Ref6]:

  • 8 KiB to 384 KiB: the rows count 4.16 to 16.66 refills per load (inner plus outer). 3.99 to 15.89 of them per load are prefetch refills. 0.17 to 0.97 per load are read refills.
  • Footprints that fit the CME L1 still bring lines from outside the cluster. From 8 KiB to 64 KiB the rows count 0.02 to 10.06 outer refills per load.
  • The source moves from inner to outer as the footprint grows. The outer refills are 6.88 per load at 32 KiB and 14.07 per load at 384 KiB.
  • 512 KiB to 32 MiB (walked once): the prefetch refills are 2.67 to 6.19 per load. The read refills are 0.9581 to 0.9987 per load.
  • The counters by source (inner, outer) and the counters by cause (read, prefetch, write) give the same total.
    • A write refill is a line brought into the CME L1 for a store. The rows count 0.0000 write refills per load in every rep row of both boots.
    • Inner plus outer minus read, prefetch and write is -0.0001 to +0.0003 per load in every rep row of boot F1.
    • It is 0.0000 per load in every rep row of boot F2.

  • The largest ratio is at 48 KiB: boot F1 takes 2.14 times the time of boot F2 (45.378 ns against 21.176 ns).

In all 11 rows every rep of one boot is above every rep of the other boot. The tables of section 4.8 have every footprint.

  • The intended difference between the two boots is one firmware setting: boot F2 turns off the data prefetchers of the cores and the prefetcher of the CME (operator's README) [Ref21].
  • Two more differences are known (section 2.2). The core commands and a self-test ran before the CME commands on boot F1 only. Each command draws its own physical pages.
  • The counters show the setting. Boot F2 counts 0.0000 prefetch refills per load in every rep row. Boot F1 counts 0.0553 to 15.8874 prefetch refills per load over the best reps.

Hypothesis

The CME prefetcher makes the random chain slower. It brings in lines that the chain does not need next. These refills delay the lines that the chain needs, or remove them from the CME L1. The counters prove the extra refills. They do not prove the delay.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A boot with only the CME prefetcher off and the core prefetchers on. The firmware turns the CME prefetcher off with bit 28 of the CME configuration register IMP_CMECFG_EL1 (operator's README) [Ref21]. If the chain load of that boot from 4 KiB to 8 MiB equals the boot F2 rows, the CME prefetcher is the cause. If it equals the boot F1 rows, the core prefetchers are the cause.

Insufficient data

Whether the lower boot F1 values at 16 MiB and 32 MiB are a gain from the prefetchers. Each setting has one boot. A second boot of each setting would give the spread from boot to boot.

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) it rises by 4.677 ns. The core rises by 6.478 ns.
  • The chain kind differs between these two footprints.
  • The number of footprints with rows of both kinds is 0.

The core rows carry other counters. The CME prefetch refill columns read n/a for the core.

  • A rep of the kind "walked many times" walks the chain 11 to 1,024 times.
  • A rep of the kind "walked once" walks its chain one time. Before the first rep the program walks another chain over the same lines two times, untimed [Ref29].
  • The largest footprint that is walked many times is 384 KiB. The smallest footprint that is walked once is 512 KiB.
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) the prefetch refills fall from 14.36 to 5.36 per load across the boundary.
Insufficient data

Whether the fall of 10.594 ns on boot F1 belongs to the footprint or to the chain kind. The number of footprints with rows of both kinds is 0. One footprint run with both chain kinds on a boot with the prefetchers on would settle it. Section 9.7 lists the hypotheses for this step.

4.6 Every line flushed first at 8 MiB, and the DRAM model

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the row with every line flushed first reads 71.714 ns per load. It counts 1.0000 outer and 0.0000 inner refills per load.
  • This is the row that the page quotes for the DRAM model.
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) the same row reads 62.080 ns. That is 4.127 ns less than the walked-once row of the same footprint.

The core, boot F144.48552.658+8.173n/an/an/a52.212

With every line flushed first, the core row counts 1.0001 read refills of the cluster L3 per load. Such a refill is a line that enters the cluster L3 for a load of the core.

  • A walk with every line flushed first removes every line from the caches before it is timed [Ref29].
  • For a buffer in the DRAM model the flush also removes the line from the SLC (project README) [Ref30].
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) that row counts 1.0000 outer, 0.0000 inner and 0.0000 prefetch refills per load. These counts are totals of a rep. They do not say which load caused which refill.
  • The 2 reps of that row differ by 0.001 ns.
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the walked-once row of 8 MiB still counts 0.0317 inner refills per load. It is 8.888 ns below the row with every line flushed first.
  • The walked-once row of 32 MiB on boot F2 reads 71.068 ns, with 0.9953 outer refills per load. That is 0.646 ns below the row with every line flushed first.
  • That row of boot F2 reads 50.709 ns above the round-trip baseline (bracket time). This is a measured difference between two kernels. It is not the access time of the DRAM model (section 4.2).
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) the walk with every line flushed first counts 2.51 prefetch refills and 0.9929 read refills per load. So the prefetcher is active in that row.
Hypothesis

On boot F2 (prefetchers off) each load of the row with every line flushed first causes one read refill. The line of that refill comes from outside the cluster.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A record of the refilled addresses of that row. The hypothesis predicts each line of the chain one time in the record, each as an outer refill.

Note

The DRAM model is a memory model of the emulator. Its 71.714 ns is not the timing of a silicon memory.

Insufficient data

Why the walk with every line flushed first is 4.127 ns faster than the walked-once row on boot F1 and slower on boot F2. No counter of these rows names the cause. The same two rows on a boot with only the CME prefetcher off would show whether the CME prefetcher makes the difference.

4.7 About one inner refill per buffer line in each timed rep (4 KiB to 64 KiB)

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off), from 4 KiB to 64 KiB, every timed rep counts about one inner refill per line of the chain.
  • The printed columns give 0.99 to 1.02 refills per line in all 21 rep rows.
  • Each value is a total of one rep: the refills per load times the loads of the rep, divided by the lines of the chain. The counters run over the whole rep [Ref33].
  • A total does not say which lines are refilled. It does not say in which walk of the rep they are refilled.
  • The footprint fits the CME L1. The program also walks the chain two times, untimed, before the first rep [Ref29]. So the rows do not show why a rep counts these refills.

Highlighted rows: the chain fits the CME L1 (4 KiB to 64 KiB). From 96 KiB on the chain does not fit the CME L1. A rep counts many refills per line there. The counter columns of the file have four decimals. So the refills per line are known to within 0.051 at 4 KiB and to within 0.003 at 64 KiB. The ns per refill est. is known to within 1.0 ns at 4 KiB and to within 0.1 ns at 64 KiB.

  • The chain load minus baseline grows with the footprint from 0.010 ns to 0.235 ns in the CME L1 rows. The refills per load grow in the same way. A larger chain is walked fewer times per rep.
  • Divided by the refills, the time above the baseline is 10.0 to 15.1 ns est. per refill from 4 KiB to 64 KiB.
  • It is 11.8 to 15.2 ns est. per refill from 96 KiB to 384 KiB, where the rows count 0.9876 to 1.0000 refills per load.
  • The estimate takes the whole measured difference between the two kernels as the cost of the refills (section 4.2).
  • Between two timed reps the program stops the counters, reads them, formats a row and starts the counters again [Ref29]. The stop, the read and the start are system calls [Ref33].
Hypothesis

Each rep starts with a CME L1 that does not hold the chain. The first walk of the rep refills every line of the chain one time. The later walks of the rep refill no line. The total of 0.99 to 1.02 inner refills per line agrees with this. It does not prove it: the same total results if some lines are refilled several times and other lines are not refilled.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A rep that counts the first walk and the later walks separately. A rep of these rows has 64 to 1,024 walks. If the first walk counts about one inner refill per line and the later walks count zero, the hypothesis holds. If the refills are spread over the walks, it is rejected. A trace of the refills by address would give the history of each line.

Hypothesis

The 0.010 to 0.235 ns above the baseline in the CME L1 rows is the cost of the about one inner refill per line that each rep counts. It is not the cost of a load that the CME L1 serves. The cost per refill supports this: its range in these rows (10.0 to 15.1 ns est.) overlaps the range of the rows that a cache inside the cluster serves (11.8 to 15.2 ns est.).

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A latency run at one footprint with twice and four times the loads per rep. If the hypothesis holds, the time above the baseline per load halves each time the walks per rep double. If it stays the same, the hypothesis is rejected.

Insufficient data

Why a rep counts about one inner refill per line of a chain that fits the CME L1. A latency run without the counters, or a rep loop with no system call between the reps, would show whether the time above the baseline disappears. Section 9.5 lists the hypotheses.

5 The cluster L3 as seen by the CME

Key points
  • Each boot has a second set of latency rows that count three L3 events of the CME (the L3-event rows). The benchmark source (file common.h) calls these three counts exploratory [Ref33]. No control row validates them.
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the chain load falls from 35.996 ns at 96 KiB (hit share 0.1434) to 32.788 ns at 256 KiB (hit share 0.6186). The 384 KiB row has the largest hit share, 0.6375, and reads 32.910 ns (best rows). The hit share is the L3 hit count divided by the sum of the L3 hit count and the L3 miss count.
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) no row counts one L3 hit per load. The largest L3 hit count there is 0.6375 per load. The two best rows with the largest counts (256 KiB and 384 KiB) take 32.788 ns to 32.910 ns. These times are 11.783 ns to 11.905 ns above the separate round-trip baseline measurement. That difference compares two kernels, and it does not isolate the time of an L3 access.
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the chain load rises by 27.003 ns from 3 MiB to 32 MiB. The outer refill count moves by 0.0578 per load over these rows, and the L3 hit count stays at or below 0.0243 per load. The counts do not explain the time there.
  • The L3-event rows repeat the times of the plain rows within 1 % at 23 of 23 footprints on boot F2 (prefetchers off) and at 20 of 23 on boot F1 (prefetchers on).

5.1 What the three events are

  • The three counts are exploratory: no control row validates them. A control row is a row whose count is known in advance.
  • The benchmark source says that no fit and no attribution may read the three counts until an independent control validates them [Ref33].
  • In every chain row of both boots the L3 refill count equals the outer refill count.
  • In the same rows the L3 hit count plus the L3 miss count equals the inner plus the outer refill count within 0.0001 per load.
  • Each count is the total of one rep divided by the number of chain loads of that rep. A count does not name the lines of the chain that the events belong to.
  • The event set cme-l3 counts seven events: the core cycle counter and six raw events [Ref33]. The six raw events are the CME cycles, the inner and outer refills, and the three L3 events.
  • The benchmark source names two checks and says that neither validates the counts [Ref33].
    • The first check compares hit plus miss with inner plus outer. The Arm manual defines the two totals over different sets of events: hit plus miss counts L3 accesses, and inner plus outer counts CME L1 refills [Ref33].
    • The agreement of the two totals is therefore not a proof. It also does not show how the total divides into hits and misses.
    • The second check is a control row: an L3 hit count of 0 on a boot whose L3 holds no data. Neither boot provides it.
  • The operator's README gives one reading of the counts. It comes from the RTL source of the CME and not from a simulation [Ref20] [Ref21].
    • By that reading the L3 hit count is the number of CME L1 refills that the cluster L3 supplied (operator's README).
    • By that reading miss minus refill is the number of refills supplied by a snoop of a core's cache in the cluster (operator's README).
    • The README states that this reading is not the independent control that the benchmark source asks for (operator's README).
  • This section therefore reports the counts and the times beside them. Every reading of a count as "the level that served the load" is inside a Hypothesis block.
  • The same holds for every reading of a count as a part of the chain or as a set of lines.

The round-trip baseline is 21.005 ns. It is a separate measurement with no memory access. Its kernel replaces the LD1D load of the chain kernel by a register copy, and both kernels return the value to the core through LASTB [Ref28]. The column "Bracket ns minus baseline" is therefore the difference between two kernels. It is not a measured time of the memory access. Counts are events per chain load: the total of the rep divided by its loads. The L3 of the cluster is 256 KiB [Ref15], and the 384 KiB footprint is larger than it. At 128 KiB, 192 KiB, 256 KiB and 384 KiB the L3 hit count plus the L3 miss count prints as 1.0000 per load, so the hit share equals the L3 hit count there. The plain rows of the same footprints read 35.979 ns (96 KiB), 35.633 ns (128 KiB), 33.910 ns (192 KiB), 32.779 ns (256 KiB), 33.014 ns (384 KiB) [Ref1].

  • Within 128 KiB, 192 KiB and 256 KiB the chain load falls from rep to rep while the L3 hit count rises.
  • At 384 KiB the chain load rises from rep to rep. The L3 hit count stays within 0.6318 to 0.6375 per load there. The outer refill count goes from 0.0417 to 0.1170 per load.

5.3 The L3-event rows of both boots

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the L3 hit count plus the L3 miss count is at most 1.0000 per load in every rep row. It is 0.9869 to 1.0000 per load from 96 KiB up (best rows).
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) the same sum reaches 16.6390 per load in the best rows and 17.0978 per load over all rep rows. It is above 1 per load at 22 of 23 footprints (best rows).
  • The rows of boot F1 (prefetchers on) therefore count more L3 accesses than chain loads. This section gives no hit share for that boot.

Times are ns per chain load: the bracket time of the best row and the span time of the same rep. Counts are events per chain load of that rep. The hit share is "n/a" where hit + miss is below 0.5 per load. It is "not given" on boot F1 (prefetchers on), where hit + miss exceeds one per load.

Hypothesis

The counts above one per load on boot F1 (prefetchers on) include refills that the hardware prefetchers cause. The same footprints on boot F2 (prefetchers off) count at most 1.0000 L3 hits plus L3 misses per load.

  • Rows that support it: the plain rows of boot F1 (prefetchers on) count 2.6629 to 16.1819 prefetch refills per load at the 22 footprints above one per load (all rep rows) [Ref5] [Ref6].
  • In those plain rows the inner plus the outer refill count equals the read refill count plus the prefetch refill count within 0.0003 per load. The read refill count is at most 0.9987 per load.
  • The L3-event rows count similar inner plus outer totals. Example, 48 KiB: 16.6381 to 17.0978 per load in the L3-event reps and 16.6606 to 16.9531 per load in the plain reps.
  • The prefetch refill count and the L3 events are in different rows. This is support and not proof.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: The prefetch refill counter of the CME (event 0x32B2) in one event set with the three L3 events on a boot with the prefetchers on [Ref33]. Neither event set of these boots holds both.

5.4 The chain load in the rows with the most L3 hits

  • The rep rows from 192 KiB to 384 KiB on boot F2 (prefetchers off) count 0.3700 to 0.6375 L3 hits per load. They take 32.788 ns to 34.592 ns. These times are 11.783 ns to 13.587 ns above the round-trip baseline (21.005 ns).
  • The round-trip baseline is a separate measurement with no memory access. Its kernel replaces the LD1D load of the chain kernel by a register copy, and both kernels return the value to the core through LASTB [Ref28].
  • Each time above the round-trip baseline in this section is therefore the measured difference between two kernels. It is not a measured time of the memory access or of an L3 hit.
  • Each of these rows counts L3 hits and L3 misses together. No row has a hit share of 1. No row therefore gives the chain load at a hit share of 1.

The rep rows of these footprints are in Table 23.

What the rows establish:

  • A chain load takes 32.788 ns to 32.910 ns when the CME counts 0.6186 to 0.6375 L3 hits per load (the best rows of 256 KiB and 384 KiB).
  • These times are 11.783 ns to 11.905 ns above the round-trip baseline of 21.005 ns. Each is the measured difference between two kernels.
  • These two rows count 0.0035 and 0.0417 outer refills per load and 0.9965 and 0.9583 inner refills per load.

What the rows do not establish:

Insufficient data

That event 0x328E counts the loads that the L3 served. The benchmark source asks for a control row: a boot whose L3 holds no data must count 0 hits [Ref33]. The L3-event rows on a boot with the L3 off would resolve it.

Insufficient data

The part of the time above the round-trip baseline that is memory-access time. The chain kernel and the round-trip kernel differ in one instruction [Ref28]. No row measures the time that the two kernels share outside the memory access. A calibration of that shared time would resolve it.

Insufficient data

Which lines of the chain the L3 hits of a row belong to. Each count is a total over one rep. A trace of the refills by address would resolve it.

Insufficient data

The chain load at a hit share of 1. The largest hit share is 0.6375. A row with an L3 hit count close to 1 per load would resolve it. One example is a chain inside the 256 KiB of the L3 that is walked many times after its lines left the caches of the core.

Insufficient data

What supplies a refill that is counted in miss minus refill. The operator's README names a snoop of a core's cache (operator's README) [Ref20] [Ref21]. No counter of these rows separates that source. A counter of the refills that a snoop of a core's cache supplies, read beside the three L3 events, would resolve it. The sources of this page name no such event number.

Insufficient data

Any time per kind of refill on boot F1 (prefetchers on). Its L3 hit count plus L3 miss count exceeds one per load. An event set with the prefetch refill counter beside the three L3 events would resolve it.

5.5 The fit of time against the counts (hypothesis)

  • A least-squares fit of the chain load against the three counts gives an estimate of the time per kind of CME L1 refill.
  • Every fitted value of this subsection is an estimate (est.). All of them belong to one hypothesis.
  • The estimate is not a result of this page. The reading of the events is not validated, and the value at a hit share of 1 lies outside the rows.
Hypothesis

On boot F2 (prefetchers off), from 96 KiB to 3 MiB, a chain load takes one fixed time per kind of CME L1 refill. The three kinds are: a refill counted as an L3 hit, a refill counted in miss minus refill, and an outer refill.

No fit of this table is a result of this page, because the events are not validated [Ref33]. The name in the first column only identifies a fit, so that the text can refer to it. The column beside it gives the rows of the fit. The text below uses fits A2, C1 and E1. a is the coefficient of the L3 hit count, b the coefficient of miss minus refill, c the coefficient of the outer refill count, each in ns per event (est.). In a fit with no intercept each coefficient is a whole chain load time (est.), not a time above the round-trip baseline. Fit C2 fits the chain load minus the round-trip baseline ("fixed"). It assumes that the round-trip baseline is an additive part of every chain load. No row establishes that. Intercept "none": the fit has no intercept. Intercept "-": the fit has a free intercept (a constant that the fit chooses) and its value is not printed. "Rms" is the residual rms and "Largest" is the largest residual. The condition number is printed twice: for the raw columns, and after each column is scaled to unit length. Coefficients printed "no (1)": the three count columns sum to about 1 per load, so a free intercept cannot be separated from the coefficients. "no (2)": the three columns move together in these rows. "no (3)": the residual rms is 6.9 ns or more, so the model does not hold above 3 MiB. "yes" means only that the coefficients can be separated numerically.

  • Fit A2 (15 rep rows, 96 KiB to 384 KiB) gives a coefficient of 29.8 ns est. per L3 hit. That is 8.8 ns est. above the round-trip baseline, which is a separate measurement of another kernel.
  • The same fit gives 37.4 ns est. per unit of miss minus refill and 44.4 ns est. per outer refill.
  • The residual rms of fit A2 is 0.089 ns and its condition number is 23.7 (3.4 with unit columns).
  • Fit C1 adds the walked-once rows up to 3 MiB (27 rep rows). It gives 29.8 ns est., 37.4 ns est. and 44.1 ns est. with a residual rms of 0.190 ns and a condition number of 2.6.
  • The coefficients of fit C1 move little when one footprint is left out (11 fits): 29.8 to 30.0 ns est. per hit, 37.2 to 37.5 ns est. per unit of miss minus refill, 43.9 to 44.2 ns est. per outer refill.
  • With one footprint left out, fit C1 predicts the rep rows of that footprint within 0.724 ns est.
  • Fit C1 reproduces a row that it was fitted on: 32.75 ns est. for the best row of 256 KiB, which measures 32.788 ns. This is not an independent check.
  • Fit E1 adds the 21 rep rows from 4 KiB to 64 KiB and a free intercept. These rows count at most 0.0156 refills per load and read 21.016 ns to 21.241 ns. They set the intercept.
  • The intercept of fit E1 is 21.007 ns est. and the round-trip baseline is 21.005 ns. The largest residual of fit E1 is 0.557 ns, so the agreement is not the precision of the fit.
  • The straight line of Figure 23 has a correlation coefficient of -0.9884 between the chain load and the L3 hit count (-1 is an exact falling line). It gives 30.7 ns est. at 1 hit per load.
  • Limit: the largest hit share of the rows is 0.6375. Every value at a hit share of 1 is an extrapolation.
  • Limit: fit C1 and fit E1 mix the two chain kinds. They assume one time per kind of refill for both.

In fits A2 and C1 the coefficient of the L3 hit count is the lowest of the three: 29.8 ns est. and 29.8 ns est. against 37.4 ns est. and 37.4 ns est. for miss minus refill, and 44.4 ns est. and 44.1 ns est. for the outer refill count. The reading of the operator's README predicts that order: by it a hit is a refill that the L3 supplied (operator's README) [Ref20] [Ref21]. The order does not validate the reading.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: Two rows are needed. First, the L3-event rows on a boot with the L3 off: the L3 hit count must read 0. Second, a row with an L3 hit count close to 1 per load: its chain load must read close to the fitted 29.8 ns est.

5.6 Where the counts stop explaining the time

  • From 512 KiB to 3 MiB on boot F2 (prefetchers off) the chain load rises from 37.589 ns to 44.069 ns as the outer refill count rises from 0.4203 to 0.9376 per load.
  • From 3 MiB to 32 MiB the chain load rises by 27.003 ns, from 44.069 ns to 71.072 ns. The outer refill count moves by 0.0578 per load and the L3 hit count stays at or below 0.0243 per load.
  • Section 9.9 shows the same rise in the plain rows, with the SLC marker and the hypothesis for it.

6 Bandwidth by footprint

Key points
  • At 4 KiB to 48 KiB, below the 64 KiB size of its L1, the CME reads 108.9 to 131.6 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 110.8 to 132.4 GB/s on boot F2 (prefetchers off) (single-call form).
  • The CME writes 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s at 4 KiB to 256 KiB on both boots (single-call form), and 39.5 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 MiB to 32 MiB (looped form).
  • At 32 MiB the read rate is 36.6 GB/s with the prefetchers on and 17.7 GB/s with the prefetchers off.
  • At 16 KiB on boot F1 (prefetchers on) the CME reads 2.14 times and writes 1.70 times the bytes per second of the core (single-call form).

Section 2.4 and section 2.5 describe the bandwidth test, its two forms and its two times. Section 7 (The cost of one kernel call) measures the time of one kernel call. Four points for reading the rates of this section:

  • Every rate of this section is a loop throughput: the bytes that the whole loop transfers, divided by the time of the loop. It is not the time that one load or one store takes to complete.
  • One iteration of the read loop runs 4 LD1B instructions, and each LD1B loads 4 vectors of 64 bytes. The same iteration runs 16 EOR instructions, which fold the loaded vectors into 16 registers (the fold). So a read rate is the rate of the loads and the EOR work together. One iteration of the write loop runs 4 ST1B instructions, and each ST1B stores 4 vectors of 64 bytes [Ref28].
  • All rates are the best row of each command, and the charts show bracket rates. Bytes per cycle (B/cycle) is the rate in GB/s divided by 2.00 cycles per ns, the measured ratio of the core cycle counter to the timer (section 2.7). So 128 GB/s is 64 B/cycle, which is one 64-byte vector per cycle.
  • These rows carry no cache counter. The program refuses its counter option together with the CME option [Ref32]. So no row of this section names the cache level that served it. The text gives footprints, and it gives the 64 KiB size of the CME L1 (operator's README) [Ref20] [Ref24] for comparison.

6.1 Read rate against footprint

  • At 4 KiB to 48 KiB, below the 64 KiB size of the CME L1, the single-call read moves 108.9 to 131.6 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 110.8 to 132.4 GB/s on boot F2 (prefetchers off). That is 54.4 to 65.8 and 55.4 to 66.2 B/cycle.
  • At footprints above that size the looped read moves 41.4 to 43.7 GB/s at 96 KiB to 256 KiB and 36.6 to 36.9 GB/s at 1 MiB to 32 MiB on boot F1 (prefetchers on). On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the 32 MiB read moves 17.7 GB/s.

  • Between 256 KiB and 1 MiB the looped read goes from 41.6 to 36.6 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on) (0.88 times) and from 41.9 to 32.8 GB/s on boot F2 (prefetchers off) (0.78 times). The write rate steps down between the same two footprints (section 6.2).

So part of the difference is inside the span. Section 7 splits the time of one call.
  • At 160 KiB and 256 KiB the two forms differ by 2.9 % and 1.6 % on boot F1 (prefetchers on): 41.4 and 41.6 GB/s (looped) against 42.6 and 42.2 GB/s (single-call). The rep spread of these four rows is 4.4 % to 6.6 % of the lowest rep. So the rows do not separate the two forms there.

The 3 reps read 60.1, 68.2, 67.4 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 37.9, 39.9, 42.8 GB/s on boot F2 (prefetchers off).
  • The single-call read at 8 KiB is lower than at 4 KiB and at 16 KiB on both boots: 108.9 GB/s against 131.6 and 120.1 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on), and 110.8 GB/s against 132.4 and 121.2 GB/s on boot F2 (prefetchers off).
Insufficient data

No bandwidth row exists between 48 KiB and 96 KiB. Single-call read rows at 56, 64, 72 and 80 KiB would show whether the first fall is at 64 KiB.

Insufficient data

No read row exists between 256 KiB and 1 MiB. Read rows at 320, 384, 512 and 768 KiB would locate the second fall.

Insufficient data

The 96 KiB single-call read row has 3 reps on each boot. The same row with 10 or more reps on each boot would show whether the difference between the boots repeats.

Insufficient data

No row explains the lower single-call read rate at 8 KiB. A CME refill counter on the bandwidth rows would show whether that row leaves the CME L1.

Section 3.3 compares these rates with two documented limits:

  • The core issues at most 2 load or store instructions per cycle to the CME (Arm Software Optimization Guide) [Ref18].
  • The LLVM model has 1 CME load pipe and 1 CME store pipe [Ref42]. A pipe is one execution unit of that model.
  • The measured single-call read at 4 KiB to 48 KiB is 0.85 to 1.03 vectors of 64 bytes per cycle on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 0.87 to 1.03 on boot F2 (prefetchers off).
Hypothesis

Section 3.3 gives the hypothesis that the load path of the CME limits the read rate at these footprints, and that the EOR work does not. The LLVM model gives 2 vectors per cycle for this kernel (est.). One vector per cycle is not the limit. The 4 KiB rows are above it. Their bracket rate is 1.03 vectors per cycle on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 1.03 on boot F2 (prefetchers off), and their span rate is 1.04 and 1.04. 10 of the 10 reps of those two rows are above one vector per cycle (bracket rate). The rows from 8 KiB to 48 KiB read 0.85 to 1.00 vectors per cycle on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 0.87 to 1.01 on boot F2 (prefetchers off). No row shows why the 4 KiB rows are the fastest.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: The read kernel also runs one EOR instruction for every loaded vector. So these rows cannot separate the load path from the EOR work. A single-call read kernel with no EOR instruction in its loop would separate them (section 3.3). A single-call read at 1 KiB and 2 KiB would show whether the rate keeps rising above one vector per cycle at small footprints.

  • The single-call write moves 51.4 to 53.7 GB/s at 4 KiB to 256 KiB on both boots. That is 25.72 to 26.86 B/cycle. The range holds on both sides of the 64 KiB size of the CME L1.
  • The looped write moves 51.5 to 52.5 GB/s at 16 KiB to 256 KiB and 39.5 to 42.6 GB/s at 1 MiB to 32 MiB on both boots. The rows do not show the cause of that step.

No write row exists between 256 KiB and 1 MiB, and no write row carries a cache counter. Write rows at 320, 384, 512 and 768 KiB would locate the step. CME refill counters on the bandwidth rows would name the level that takes the stored lines. No write row of this page is labelled with a destination level.

6.3 Copy rows

  • The copy moves 105.3 GB/s at 16 KiB and 103.1 GB/s at 48 KiB on boot F1 (prefetchers on). The rate counts the bytes read plus the bytes written [Ref32].
  • From 96 KiB to 32 MiB the copy moves 40.1 to 42.2 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on). On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the 32 MiB copy moves 34.2 GB/s, 0.83 times the boot F1 (prefetchers on) rate.

Rates count bytes read plus bytes written. B/cycle is from the bracket rate. The full tables of section 6.8 give three decimals.

  • The 48 KiB copy touches two buffers of 48 KiB, which is 96 KiB in total. It moves 103.1 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on), against 105.3 GB/s for the 16 KiB copy.
  • Half of a copy rate is bytes written. At 16 KiB and 48 KiB that half is 52.6 and 51.5 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on). The looped write kernel moves 52.4 and 51.6 GB/s at the same footprints.
  • So at 16 KiB and 48 KiB the written half of the copy equals the rate of the write kernel alone within 0.2 GB/s.
  • At 96 KiB the copy moves 42.2 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on), of which 21.1 GB/s is bytes read. The looped read kernel moves 43.7 GB/s at 96 KiB.
  • So from 96 KiB to 2 MiB the read half of the copy is 0.48 to 0.61 times the rate of the read kernel alone (both boots). At 32 MiB it is 0.56 times on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 0.97 times on boot F2 (prefetchers off).
Insufficient data

Why the read half of a copy above the CME L1 is slower than the read kernel alone. The copy rows carry no counter. CME refill counters on a copy row would show whether the loads or the stores of the copy wait for refills (section 9.10).

Hypothesis

Stored lines do not take CME L1 space the way loaded lines do. Under that reading only the 48 KiB source buffer has to fit in the 64 KiB L1.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: CME refill counters on the copy rows at 48 KiB and 96 KiB. A count near 0 refills per line at 48 KiB would confirm it.

Insufficient data

The copy kernel exists in the looped form only, at 16 KiB to 32 MiB. The boots have no single-call copy row, no copy row at 4, 8 or 24 KiB, and no copy row on OCM. Those rows would be needed to give a copy rate without one kernel call per pass.
