6.5 The 64-byte forms

The main read and write kernels move 256 bytes per instruction (four vectors). The kernels cme-ldr16 and cme-str16 move 64 bytes per instruction (one vector) [Ref28]. Their CSV names come from the core kernels. They do not mean 16 bytes.

  • The 64-byte write is within 0.6 % of the 256-byte write at all 3 footprints on boot F1 (prefetchers on). On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the largest difference is 6.9 %, at 2 MiB.
  • The 64-byte read at 16 KiB moves 46.7 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 56.3 GB/s on boot F2 (prefetchers off). The 256-byte read of the same file moves 52.2 and 50.4 GB/s. So the 64-byte form is 0.90 times the 256-byte form on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 1.12 times on boot F2 (prefetchers off).
  • A second looped 16 KiB read row of the 256-byte form is in cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv [Ref43] [Ref47]. It reads 53.0 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 53.1 GB/s on boot F2 (prefetchers off). Against that row the 64-byte form is 0.88 times on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 1.06 times on boot F2 (prefetchers off).

6.7 Lines in flight (est.)

  • A line request is in flight between the moment the CME sends it and the moment the line arrives.
  • The looped read has an effective time per 64 bytes transferred: 64 divided by its rate in GB/s, in ns. It is a throughput of the whole loop, not the time of one load.
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the chain load time is 19.7 to 22.0 times that effective time (est.), at 256 KiB, 2 MiB and 32 MiB.
  • This ratio is an estimate of how many line requests overlap in a looped read. No row measures that number.
Hypothesis

Table 35. Hypothesis table. Chain load time divided by the effective time per 64 bytes transferred of the looped read at the same footprint and boot (est.). Chain load: [Ref1] [Ref3] [Ref5] [Ref6]. Read rate: cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv [Ref13] [Ref14].

Boot F1 (prefetchers on)
256 KiBwalked many times51.10041.561.54033.219.5
2 MiBwalked once56.10336.921.73332.420.2
32 MiBwalked once70.48236.581.74940.328.3

Effective time per 64 B transferred = 64 / rate in GB/s. It is a throughput of the whole read loop, not the time of one load. The ratio columns are estimates. The last column subtracts the round-trip baseline of 21.005 ns, a separate measurement with no memory access, from the chain load time. All times are bracket times of the best row. The 256 KiB chain load comes from cme-latency-dram-small.csv, the 2 MiB and 32 MiB chain loads from cme-latency-dram-large.csv.

With the prefetchers off the CME keeps between 8 and 22 line requests in flight during a looped read (est.). The upper value is the ratio with the whole chain load time, which is 19.7 to 22.0 on boot F2 (prefetchers off) at the 3 footprints. On boot F1 (prefetchers on) that ratio is 32.4 to 40.3, and the prefetchers add requests of their own there.

Every chain load returns its result to the core through LASTB. A looped read does not. The round-trip baseline is a separate measurement with no memory access, and it reads 21.005 ns per step. The lower value subtracts that baseline from the chain load time. That subtraction is the measured difference between two kernels. The rows do not show that it is the time of the memory access alone. With the baseline subtracted the boot F2 (prefetchers off) ratios are 7.7, 11.2, 13.8 (est.), and they rise with the footprint. So the rows do not show one fixed number. The 3 chain loads are also not of one chain kind. The 256 KiB chain is walked many times. The 2 MiB chain is walked once. The 32 MiB chain is walked once.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A latency test that walks N independent chains in the same loop, for N from 1 to 32. The loads per second stop rising at the N that equals the number of requests in flight.

Insufficient data

The chain-load kernel and the round-trip baseline kernel share work that is not a memory access. No row measures that shared work. A calibration of it would be needed to call the chain load minus the baseline a memory-access time, and to choose between the two ratios of this section.

7 The cost of one kernel call

Key points
  • One looped 4 KiB read call on boot F1 (prefetchers on) takes 218.1 ns. The span holds 134.8 ns of it. The other 83.2 ns is outside-span time.
  • The single-call form reads the same 4 KiB in 31.1 ns per pass. So a looped rate at a small footprint mostly measures the fixed time of a call (entry, exit, fold and stamps), not the throughput of the read loop.
  • A call of loads that stands alone in its bracket spends 286.0 ns outside its span (median, boot F1). Calls that follow each other spend 63.5 to 64.6 ns on the cme-call rows (both boots). They spend 76.0 to 106.2 ns on the looped bandwidth rows up to 256 KiB (boot F1). No row shows the cause of the difference.
  • A fitted cost per call can be quoted only where the fit passes the plan rule. 3 of the 4 fits of the looped read pass. All four fits of the looped write are void.

7.1 One looped read call, to scale

  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) a looped 4 KiB read call spends 38 % of its bracket time outside the span.
  • Inside the span, 103.9 ns est. does not grow with the bytes. The loop over the 64 vectors of 64 bytes takes the other 30.9 ns est.

A kernel here is one test loop in cme_kern.S, not the Linux kernel. Each kernel call saves registers, enters streaming mode with SMSTART, takes the first stamp, runs its loop, takes the second stamp, leaves streaming mode with SMSTOP and restores the registers [Ref28]. The span time is the time between the two stamps. The bracket time is measured by two clock reads in C around all calls of a rep [Ref32]. The outside-span time is the bracket time minus the span time. The rows hold one bracket total and one span total per rep. So a time per call is an average over the calls of the rep.

7.2 Time per pass against bytes per pass

  • The looped read lies on a straight line that meets the time axis at 186.2 ns est. (bracket) and 103.9 ns est. (span) on boot F1 (prefetchers on).
  • That intercept is the fixed time of one looped read call on boot F1 (prefetchers on), fold and stamps included. It is not the cost of a call in general. A call with one register step takes 124.5 to 125.6 ns (section 7.5).
  • The points of the looped write, the looped write with DSB ST and the single-call read do not lie on one line. All their fits are void. No line is drawn for them.

Each chart plots the time of one pass against the bytes of one pass at 4 KiB, 8 KiB, 16 KiB and 24 KiB. All four footprints fit in the CME L1. A straight line through the four points has two parts. The intercept is the time of a pass of 0 bytes. The slope gives the rate. In the looped form a pass is one call, so the intercept is the fixed time per call of that kernel. Every intercept and every fitted rate is an estimate (est.). The plan rule decides whether a fit counts [Ref49]. Two control rows exist beside the looped read and the looped write. The no-fold read leaves out the fold (the XOR of all loaded words into one value) at the end of each call. The DSB ST write adds a store barrier before the second stamp, inside the span [Ref28].

7.4 The call-cost rows: short calls, in ns per call

  • A 1 KiB read call takes 186.1 ns on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 191.1 ns on boot F2 (prefetchers off). A 1 KiB write call takes 124.1 ns on both boots.
  • A write call of 8 times the bytes takes only 1.47 x (boot F1) and 1.35 x (boot F2) the time.
  • The single-call form writes 53.7 GB/s at 4 KiB on boot F1 (prefetchers on). At that rate the write loop moves 1 KiB in 19.1 ns est. The call takes 124.1 ns. So most of the time of a short call does not grow with its bytes. Section 7.8 shows why the write rows cannot give the exact share.

The bracket and span times of the best rep are the bytes per call divided by the rates of the best row (5 significant digits). The outside-span times use the span_s column of each rep. So the outside-span time of a row can differ by 0.01 ns from its bracket time minus its span time.

  • The span of a write call grows by 18.1 ns from 4 KiB to 8 KiB on boot F1 (prefetchers on) (17.8 ns on boot F2). The added 4,096 bytes would then move at 226 GB/s est. That is 4.3 x the 52.2 GB/s of the single-call form at 8 KiB. Section 7.8 treats this.

The other four have spans of 237.8 to 238.6 ns and outside-span times of 76.9 to 77.1 ns. The bracket time is 313.8 to 315.6 ns in all five. So in that row the higher level is not extra time. The span is 15.4 ns shorter in that rep.
Insufficient data

No row shows the cause of the two levels on boot F1 (prefetchers on). These rows carry no counters. Ten reps per row would show whether the two levels are stable. A CME cycle count per call on a bandwidth row would show whether the core or the CME spends the extra 14.2 ns of the 8 KiB call-cost row.

7.5 The cme-call rows: the shortest call

  • A call that does one register step takes 124.5 to 125.6 ns over the 24 files of both boots.
  • Its span is 61.00 ns in 68 of the 72 reps (highest 61.25 ns). Its outside-span time is 63.5 to 64.6 ns.

A cme-call row times 64 kernel calls in one bracket, each call directly after the one before it [Ref29]. Each call runs one step of the round-trip baseline. That step moves a value from a core register to a CME register and back. The row has no memory access. So it gives the time of a call whose only work is one register step.

Insufficient data

The round-trip baseline is a separate measurement. Its time per step is an average over a long loop. The rows do not show that the one step of a cme-call call takes that time. So the span of a cme-call call cannot be split into one step and a fixed rest. A cme-call row whose kernel runs no step would give the span of a call without the step.

An OCM latency pass is one kernel call in its own bracket, with a counter start before it. A single-call bandwidth rep is one kernel call in its own bracket, after one untimed pass, with no counter call.

  • A bracket also holds its two clock reads. They take 39.0 ns on both boots in an empty bracket [Ref25]. One file of boot F2 prints 40.0 ns. A lone call carries all of that time. A call of a cme-call row carries 1/64 of it (0.6 ns). So 38.4 ns est. of the difference is clock-read time. 184.0 ns est. (boot F1) and 183.3 ns est. (boot F2) remain without a cause.
  • The lone calls of the single-call read rows spend 280.0 to 300.9 ns outside the span in the reps after the first, on both boots. The bandwidth program runs no counter call. It refuses the counter option together with the CME option [Ref32]. So a counter call before the bracket cannot be the only cause of the extra time.
  • The first rep of a single-call read row spends 339.9 to 408.0 ns. That is more than the reps after it spend.
  • A lone write call spends more than a lone read call. In the reps after the first, the single-call write rows spend 354.6 to 427.8 ns on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 371.0 to 421.0 ns on boot F2 (prefetchers off). The medians are 96.8 ns and 98.3 ns above the lone read call. Insufficient data: no row shows why. Section 7.8 gives a hypothesis about stores that end after the span.
  • On a pass of 64 loads, 286.0 ns is 4.5 ns per load. The bracket value of such a row lies above its span value by that amount.
  • The outside-span time per looped call is higher in the rows with fewer calls per rep. It is 118.5 to 398.0 ns per call at 1 to 32 MiB over both boots, where a rep is 8, 4 or 2 calls. In these rows the footprint grows and the number of calls per rep falls together. So the rows do not show which of the two sets the time.
Hypothesis

A cost that is paid once per bracket is divided by fewer calls in the rows of 1 MiB and more. The two clock reads of the bracket are one such cost.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: The 32 MiB row with 16 passes per rep. An outside-span time per call near that of the rows up to 256 KiB confirms it. An unchanged time per call rejects it.

Section 9.4 gives the hypotheses for the extra time of a lone call, each with the measurement that would confirm or reject it.

7.7 The CME cycle counter gap

  • Per counting window the CME cycle count is 583 to 603 cycles below the core cycle count (medians of the three kinds of row on both boots). At the measured 2.000 cycles per ns that is 291.5 to 301.5 ns.
  • A link between that amount and the time of a lone call is a hypothesis.
  • A row gives four totals per pass: two cycle counts, one bracket time and one span time. It gives no time stamp of a counter start or stop. So the figure below compares the four totals as durations. It does not place the CME cycle count inside the bracket.

The latency rows count core cycles and CME cycles over the counting window. The counting window is the interval between the counter start and the counter stop of one row. Both counts are totals [Ref33]. Both counters are opened with the kernel-mode exclusion flag [Ref33]. The order of the code is: counter start, first clock read, kernel call, second clock read, counter stop [Ref29]. The two stamps of the span are executed inside the kernel call [Ref28]. So the order of the code places the span between the two clock reads, and the two clock reads between the counter start and the counter stop. The order of the code does not place the CME cycle count. The rows do not show in which part of the window the CME cycles are counted.

The table below gives the core cycle count minus the CME cycle count per window. At the measured 2.000 cycles per ns, 600 cycles are 300 ns. The same ratio converts the CME cycle count. In the rows of 8,192 loads or more the CME cycle count divided by the span time is 2.000 to 2.001 cycles per ns on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 1.999 to 2.001 cycles per ns on boot F2 (prefetchers off).

At that ratio the CME cycle counter also counts outside the spans of calls that follow each other.
  • The difference of the two counts is taken against the core cycle count. The core cycle count, converted to time, is above the bracket time by a median of 91.3 to 101.4 ns (boot F1).
  • The bracket time is above the CME cycle count, converted to time, by a median of 201.5 to 205.9 ns (boot F1).

Insufficient data

The rows give totals. They give no time stamp of the counter start, of the counter stop, or of the first and the last cycle that the CME cycle counter counts. A timer read beside the counter start and beside the counter stop would place the core cycle count against the bracket. A counting window with no kernel call in it, with both cycle counts printed, would show whether the CME cycle counter counts outside a call.

What the gap means is not measured. Section 9.4 gives three readings of it as hypotheses (the clock of the CME does not run before the first call of a window, the CME leaves a low-power state, or the two counters do not start at the same instant), each with the measurement that would confirm or reject it.

7.8 The looped write: a span rate above the single-call rate

  • At 8 KiB the span rate of a looped write call is 93.5 GB/s on boot F1 (prefetchers on). The single-call form writes 52.2 GB/s at the same footprint. The span rate is 1.79 x the single-call rate.
  • At 16 KiB and 24 KiB a looped write pass takes the bracket time of a single-call pass within 2.0 ns (-2.0 to -0.7 ns on boot F1, -1.4 to -0.3 ns on boot F2), although it makes one call per pass.
  • The four points do not lie on a line. The plan rule voids every looped write fit.

The boot F1 16 KiB looped span is that of the rep with the best bracket rate. The other four reps have spans of 237.8 to 238.6 ns (68.7 to 68.9 GB/s).

  • At 4 KiB the looped pass takes 75.6 ns more than the single-call pass on boot F1 (prefetchers on) (73.1 ns on boot F2).
  • At 8 KiB the difference is 6.9 ns. At 16 KiB and 24 KiB it is -2.0 to -0.7 ns (boot F1).
  • Each of those looped calls still spends 76.2 to 91.6 ns outside its span (best reps, boot F1).
  • With DSB ST the pass takes 47.4, 97.8, 76.9 and 74.3 ns longer at 4 KiB, 8 KiB, 16 KiB and 24 KiB on boot F1 (prefetchers on). The outside-span time of one looped write call at 16 KiB and 24 KiB is 76.9 to 91.9 ns over all reps.
Hypothesis

The span of a write call ends before its stores are complete. The last stores of a call finish while the call leaves streaming mode and the next call enters it. So the cost of the call overlaps with store work, and the span is shorter than the store work it started. The DSB ST rows are consistent with this reading. They do not prove it. The barrier adds 74.3 to 76.9 ns at 16 KiB and 24 KiB (boot F1), but the rows do not show that this time is the wait for the stores of the call [Ref49].

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A waveform of the store interface of the CME over one 8 KiB call would show when the last store completes against the second stamp. The run plan names no row that could identify the mechanism from timing alone [Ref49].

Section 9.3 lists the measurements that would settle this.

7.9 What can be quoted, and what cannot

  • Quote a time per call only together with its form, its footprint, its boot and its clock.
  • Do not quote a fixed cost per call for writes. Do not quote any number as the cost of SMSTART and SMSTOP alone.
  • Section 3.5 lists the numbers of the whole page that are not to be quoted. Section 9.13 lists the statements that the rows do not support.

8 OCM through the CME

Key points
  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) every pass of the OCM rows counts 1.0000 outer refills and 0.0000 prefetch refills per load. A chain load takes 43.453 to 44.391 ns of span time for regions 0 to 2 and 47.266 to 47.734 ns for regions 3 and 4.
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) no OCM row is demand-only. The one-region rows read 32.812 to 34.688 ns of span time with 0.22 to 0.58 prefetch refills per load.
  • The CME reads one OCM region at 33.6 to 39.8 GB/s on boot F1 and at 27.7 to 33.9 GB/s on boot F2.
  • The CME writes all five regions at 30.7 GB/s on boot F1 and at 31.0 GB/s on boot F2. There is no write row for one region.
  • In 20 of 20 one-region commands the home node of the region receives the most requests. The mesh counts are totals over the whole command.

Each timed rep of an OCM latency row is one pass over its chain. So this section calls a timed rep of these rows a pass, and "pass 1" is the row cme-fresh1 of a file, "pass 2" the row cme-fresh2, and so on.

8.1 The mesh and the five OCM regions

  • Each OCM region sits in one home node of the 6 x 6 mesh. The node id gives the position of the home node.
  • The position of DSU 1 at crosspoint (2,3) is a hypothesis. From there regions 0 to 2 are 1 step away and regions 3 and 4 are 3 steps away.

  • Each region is 256 KiB long, which is 64 pages of 4 KiB. One page holds 64 lines of 64 bytes.
  • The map shows a home node at each of the five decoded positions [Ref15].
  • The map does not say which cluster port belongs to which cluster.
  • The project file README.md states the step counts from CPU 2: one step to the home nodes of regions 0 to 2 and three steps to the home nodes of regions 3 and 4 [Ref30].
  • The README gives notes of the operator as its source for these step counts. It names no design file.
  • Only 1 of the 5 cluster ports gives these step counts (Table 49).

Hypothesis

DSU 1 (CPUs 2 and 3 and their CME) uses the cluster port at crosspoint (2,3).

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A file that names the mesh port of each cluster would confirm or reject it. The device tree or the mesh configuration of the chip is such a file. Neither is in the result folders.

Insufficient data

The origin of the step counts in the project file README.md [Ref30]. The file does not say whether they come from the chip design or from latency rows. If they come from latency rows, the time difference between the regions (section 8.3) is not independent support for them. The mesh configuration of the chip would resolve it.

8.2 Chain load per region, both boots

  • A chain load from OCM takes 43.453 to 47.734 ns of span time on boot F2 (prefetchers off). Every pass of these rows counts 0.0000 prefetch refills per load.
  • The same rows read 32.812 to 43.658 ns on boot F1 (prefetchers on). Their passes count 0.22 to 1.27 prefetch refills per load. Boot F2 is 1.29 to 1.39 times boot F1 for one region.
  • Every OCM row is a chain that is walked once, with every line flushed first.
  • Each timed pass walks a chain that no pass walked before. So one timed pass is one rep, which is one data row of the CSV file.
  • The rows have two shapes. The shape "one line per 4 KiB page" has 64 loads per region and pass. The shape "every line" has 20,480 loads over all five regions.
  • The figure uses span time. One pass is one kernel call.
  • A call spends 280 to 304 ns outside its span in the one-region rows (all 70 passes of both boots). Divided by the 64 loads of a pass, that is 4.38 to 4.75 ns per load.
  • The best bracket time of a one-region row is 4.38 to 4.52 ns per load above its best span time (Table 50).
  • The span value of a row is the lowest span time over its passes.

Span time: lowest over the passes. Bracket time: the cme-best row of the program. The round-trip baseline is 21.001 ns of span time in these files. It is a separate measurement with no memory access (instructions DUP and LASTB). The chain kernel has the instructions LD1D and LASTB. So the column "span time minus the round-trip baseline" is the difference between two kernels. It is not the time of the OCM access alone. The one-region rows have the shape "one line per 4 KiB page".

Insufficient data

What part of the span time minus the round-trip baseline is the time of the OCM access is not known. The chain kernel and the baseline kernel share the instruction LASTB and the loop. No row measures the time of the part that they share. A calibration of the non-memory time that the two kernels share would give it.

  • On boot F2 the two shapes differ by 0.212 ns. The all-five rows read 45.744 ns (one line per 4 KiB page) and 45.532 ns (every line) of span time. The mean of the five one-region rows is 45.441 ns.
  • On boot F1 the two shapes differ by 8.252 ns. The row with every line reads 43.658 ns and the row with one line per 4 KiB page reads 35.406 ns.
  • The boot F1 row with every line counts 0.9599 to 0.9621 read refills, 1.24 to 1.27 prefetch refills and 1.91 to 1.93 outer refills per load.
  • Every pass of boot F2 is slower than every pass of boot F1, in all 7 rows.
Hypothesis

Most lines that the prefetcher brings in the boot F1 row with every line are not the next member of the chain.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A count of the chain loads that find their line in the CME L1 would confirm or reject it. The files hold refill counts only.

Insufficient data

The cost of address translation in these rows is not known. The OCM rows use 4 KiB pages and carry no counter of translation misses. The same OCM rows on a mapping with larger pages, on a boot with the prefetchers off, would give it.

8.3 Time against mesh steps on boot F2

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the regions at 3 steps read 3.432 ns more span time than the regions at 1 step (means 47.500 ns and 44.068 ns).
  • Every pass of regions 3 and 4 (47.266 to 48.016 ns) is slower than every pass of regions 0 to 2 (43.453 to 44.719 ns).
  • The two groups are an observation by region: regions 3 and 4 against regions 0 to 2.
  • The step counts depend on the hypothesis of the position of DSU 1, and the origin of the stated step counts is not known (section 8.1). So mesh steps are one hypothesis for the two groups.
  • The best values of boot F1 do not separate the two groups. Regions 0 to 2 read 32.812 to 34.359 ns and regions 3 and 4 read 34.312 to 34.688 ns there.
  • The medians of boot F1 separate the two groups. They are 34.484 to 35.516 ns for regions 0 to 2 and 37.953 to 38.094 ns for regions 3 and 4 (Table 51).
  • The pass ranges of boot F1 overlap (32.812 to 39.656 ns and 34.312 to 43.062 ns). So boot F1 cannot give a cost per step.
Hypothesis

The 3.432 ns difference is the cost of 2 more mesh steps on the way to the home node and 2 more on the way back. That is 1.72 ns per step of distance (est.), request and data together.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: The same rows from the CME of another cluster would confirm or reject it. The step counts to the five regions differ there (Table 49).

8.4 Pass values and spread

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) the passes of a one-region row lie within 0.35 to 0.81 % of each other (span time).
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) they lie 9.3 to 25.5 % apart.

8.5 What the refill counters show

  • On boot F2 (prefetchers off) every pass of all 7 rows counts 1.0000 read refills, 1.0000 outer refills, 0.0000 inner refills and 0.0000 prefetch refills per load.
  • A one-region pass of boot F2 has 64 loads. Each of the 35 one-region passes of boot F2 counts 64 read refills, 64 outer refills and 0 prefetch refills.
  • These counts are totals of a pass. They do not say which load caused which refill.
  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) every pass counts prefetch refills (0.22 to 0.58 per load in the one-region rows).
  • On boot F1 a pass with fewer read refills is faster. The correlation coefficient between read refills per load and span time is +0.906 over the 35 one-region passes (+1 is an exact rising line).

Read refills plus prefetch refills equal inner refills plus outer refills within 0.0001 per load in every pass of both boots.

Hypothesis

On boot F2 each timed load causes one read refill of the CME L1, and the line of that refill comes from outside the cluster.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A record of the refills by address would confirm or reject it. The files hold one count per pass.

Hypothesis

A chain load that causes no read refill takes about as long as one step of the round-trip baseline. A chain load that causes a read refill from OCM takes about 23.1 ns more (est.). The line of Figure 46 gives 23.10 ns at 0 read refills (est.). That is 2.10 ns above the round-trip baseline of 21.001 ns.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A time stamp per load, or a row in which every line is prefetched before the timed pass, would confirm or reject it.

8.6 The core beside the CME on boot F1

  • On boot F1 (prefetchers on) a chain load from one OCM region takes 18.656 to 22.609 ns on the core (CPU 2) and 32.812 to 34.688 ns of span time through the CME. The CME is 1.53 to 1.76 times the core.
  • The core row with every line is demand-only and reads 25.536 ns. The CME row with every line on boot F2 is also demand-only and reads 45.532 ns. That is 19.996 ns more.
  • The difference of 19.996 ns is 1.005 ns below the round-trip baseline of 21.001 ns.
  • Put the other way, the boot F2 CME row minus the round-trip baseline is 24.531 ns, and the core row reads 25.536 ns.
  • The round-trip baseline is a separate measurement with no memory access. The rows do not show that a chain load contains the baseline time as a fixed part.

  • The write rate is the same on both boots within 1.1 %.
  • The read rates of boot F2 are not ordered by mesh steps. Regions 0 to 2 read 27.7 to 33.9 GB/s and regions 3 and 4 read 30.1 to 31.1 GB/s.
  • Put as bracket time per 64 bytes transferred, a one-region read is 1.61 to 1.90 ns through the CME on boot F1, 1.89 to 2.31 ns on boot F2 and 3.18 to 3.22 ns on the core.
  • That value is the bracket time of the best pass divided by the 4,096 lines of the region. It is a rate of the whole loop. It is not the time that one load instruction takes.
  • One loop iteration of the CME read kernel loads 1,024 bytes with four instructions and runs 16 EOR instructions [Ref28].
  • A read row has 3 reps. Each rep is 1 pass.
  • The reps of a one-region row differ by 1.1 to 26.7 %. So the best value of a row is one single pass, and no other rep repeats it.
Insufficient data

The write rate of one OCM region is not measured. Each boot holds one write row, over all five regions (cme-bandwidth-ocm-write.csv). The write command on one region would give it.

Kernel calls per pass. The bandwidth program calls the kernel once per region of the buffer [Ref32]. So a pass over all five regions is 5 kernel calls. A write rep of 8 passes is 40 kernel calls. Table 55 gives the outside-span time per kernel call.

"Per call" means per kernel call. Bracket time per pass is of the best rep. 1 us = 1,000 ns. Outside-span time = bracket time minus the span_s column. The elapsed_s column of the files has steps of 1 us. So the bracket time of a rep is rebuilt as total_bytes divided by aggregate_GBps. That rate has three decimals. The rebuilt bracket time of a rep is therefore known to 0.2 ns (est.) for a one-region read, to 0.6 ns (est.) for the all-five read and to 6 ns (est.) for a write rep of 8 passes.   • A one-region read call spends 328 to 485 ns outside its span.
  • The first rep is the highest in all 10 one-region files (424 to 485 ns). The later reps read 328 to 374 ns.
  • Every rep follows a flush of the region. So the flush alone does not explain the higher first rep.
  • A call of the all-five read spends 136 to 155 ns outside its span. A call of the write spends 88 to 94 ns.
  • Within one rep the outside-span time is at most 6.6 % of the bracket time, in every row of both boots.
Insufficient data

Why the first rep of a one-region read spends more time outside its span is not known. The files hold no counter for the time outside the span. A run with one untimed kernel call before the first rep would show whether the first call of a command costs more.

Insufficient data

The bandwidth files hold no refill counters. So they cannot say what share of the lines of a boot F1 read came by prefetch. A CME bandwidth run with the refill events of the CME L1 counted would give it.

Insufficient data

These rows cannot be compared with the bandwidth rows on the DRAM model under equal conditions. An OCM read rep is one pass after a flush of every line. The rows on the DRAM model run several passes with no flush. Rows on the DRAM model with one pass after a flush, at 256 KiB and at 1.25 MiB, would give the comparison.

8.8 Mesh counters: where the requests arrive

  • In 20 of the 20 one-region commands the home node with the most requests received is the node that holds the region of the command. So the requests of each command arrive mainly at its intended home node.
  • Every mesh count of this section is a total over the whole command. It is not a count of the timed passes.
  • Over the whole command that node receives more requests than the mean count of the other four nodes. The difference, divided by the 4,096 lines of the region, is 8.4 to 18.4 requests per line.
  • That value is a total divided by a line count. It is not the number of requests that each line or each load causes.
  • It receives 4.6 to 12.7 times the count of the next node.
  • Which control is subtracted. The level subtracted in a row is the mean count of the four home nodes that do not hold the region, in the same command.
  • An idle control is a mesh count of a small command that sends almost no requests to the home nodes. No idle control was taken with a CME command.
  • Boot F2 has no idle control in its mesh counter file.
  • Boot F1 has 4 counted idle controls, one per CPU (labels control-cpu2, control-cpu4, control-cpu6, control-cpu8). This section uses the one of CPU 2 (control-cpu2), the CPU that runs the CME commands.
  • That idle control is the core latency program on a 4 KiB buffer in the DRAM model. It runs for 1.239 ms [Ref37].
  • That idle control counts 7,348 to 7,490 requests per node. The four other nodes of the boot F1 one-region commands count 425 to 1,922 more than it. The excess of the intended node is 36,768 to 75,239 requests.
  • The counters run for the whole command lifetime. That covers the fill of the buffer, the build of the chains, the untimed walks, every flush and the timed passes.
  • The counts cannot be limited to the timed loads.
  • So the figure gives requests per line of the region, not per timed load. A latency command has 448 timed loads, which is 1.1 to 1.3 % of its excess.
  • For the timed passes the files hold the CME counters only. Every pass on boot F2 counts 1.0000 outer refills per load (Table 52).

8.9 Mesh requests of the 8 MiB command, prefetchers on against off

  • During the latency command on an 8 MiB buffer in the DRAM model, with every line flushed first, the five home nodes receive 53.87 requests per line of the buffer on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and 34.52 on boot F2 (prefetchers off).
  • The five home nodes receive 1.56 times as many requests on boot F1 (prefetchers on) as on boot F2 (prefetchers off) during the same command.

The 2,535,995 more requests on boot F1 (19.35 per line) are requests of the hardware prefetchers.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: Mesh counters that run around the timed pass only would confirm or reject it. A mesh event that counts prefetch requests apart from read requests would do the same.

9 Open items and what was not measured

Key points
  • Nine observations on boot F1 (prefetchers on) and boot F2 (prefetchers off) have no measured cause.
  • The first one is a step of the CME write rate. It reads 51.5 to 52.5 GB/s from 16 KiB to 256 KiB and 39.5 to 42.6 GB/s from 1 MiB to 32 MiB.
  • 15 kinds of row do not exist on these boots (section 9.11).

9.1 The write rate steps down between 256 KiB and 1 MiB

  • The CME write rate is 51.5 to 52.5 GB/s from 16 KiB to 256 KiB and 39.5 to 42.6 GB/s from 1 MiB to 32 MiB, on both boots (looped form, bracket time, file cme-bandwidth-dram-1core.csv [Ref13] [Ref14]).
  • No CME bandwidth row has a refill counter. No write row on a buffer in the DRAM model ran under the mesh counters. So no cache level can be named for either rate.
  • The figure and the table of these rows are in section 6.2. The core rows are in section 6.4.

Observation

  • The 1 MiB rate is 0.793 times the 256 KiB rate on boot F1 and 0.787 times on boot F2.
  • The single-call form reads the same inside the span: 51.6 to 52.6 GB/s from 48 KiB to 256 KiB on boot F1 and 51.8 to 52.5 GB/s on boot F2 (file cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv [Ref11] [Ref12]).
  • The write rate does not step at 64 KiB, the size of the CME L1 (operator's README) [Ref20]. It reads 51.6 GB/s at 48 KiB and 52.4 GB/s at 96 KiB on boot F1.
  • The read rate does step there: 87.2 GB/s at 48 KiB and 43.7 GB/s at 96 KiB on boot F1.
  • The write of the core on boot F1 reads 30.6 to 32.0 GB/s from 16 KiB to 32 MiB and has no step (file bandwidth-dram-1core.csv [Ref53]).
  • Both boots show the step. So the prefetcher setting alone does not cause it.

Why it is not explained

  • The bandwidth program refuses its counter option together with the CME option [Ref32]. So no bandwidth row has a CME counter.
  • No row lies between 256 KiB and 1 MiB. So the footprint at which the rate steps is not known.
  • 15 CME commands per boot ran under the mesh counters. The OCM write is the only write among them [Ref22] [Ref23].

Hypotheses

Hypothesis

Up to 256 KiB, the size of the cluster L3, the written lines stay inside the cluster. Above it, each pass sends written lines out to the mesh, and that path limits the rate.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: CME write rows at footprints between 256 KiB and 1 MiB, under the mesh counters. The hypothesis predicts that the mesh requests per pass rise at the footprint where the rate steps.

Hypothesis

Above the step, the limit is the rate at which the cluster obtains the right to write a line (ownership) from outside the cluster. The eviction of written lines is not the limit.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: CME refill counters on a bandwidth write row. A count near one outer refill per line above the step, with a rate that follows the refill latency, would support it.

Hypothesis

The rate below the step is a store-rate limit of the CME and has no relation to a cache level (see section 9.2).

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A store-path counter of the CME on a write row, or the store timing in the RTL. The flat rate across the 64 KiB size of the CME L1 is consistent with this hypothesis and does not prove it.

What would settle it

  • CME write rows at footprints between 256 KiB and 1 MiB.
  • The same rows under the mesh counters, to compare the mesh requests per pass at 256 KiB and at 1 MiB.
  • CME counters on a bandwidth row. The program does not offer this.

9.2 The read loop transfers more bytes per cycle than the write loop

  • At 16 KiB the read throughput divided by the write throughput is 2.31 on boot F1 and 2.33 on boot F2 (single-call form, span time).
  • Each throughput is the bytes of a whole loop divided by its time. Each load or store instruction of these loops transfers four 64-byte vectors. The read loop also runs the XOR instructions of the fold [Ref28].
  • So these numbers do not give the time that one load or one store takes.
  • The buffer is 16 KiB and the CME L1 is 64 KiB (operator's README) [Ref20]. So a refill is not expected in these rows. No bandwidth row has a refill counter to confirm that.

Table 61. Single-call read and write at 16 KiB, best rows (cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv).

BootRead,

Boot F1 (prefetchers on)121.107 GB/s52.342 GB/s1.062.452.31

Effective cycles per 64 bytes transferred = 64 bytes / span rate x 2.00 core cycles per ns. It is a loop throughput and not the time of one load or one store.

Observation

  • The single-call read reads 121.1 GB/s on boot F1 and 122.2 GB/s on boot F2 in the span.
  • The single-call write reads 52.3 GB/s and 52.5 GB/s.
  • In the single-call form from 4 KiB to 48 KiB the write loop needs 2.38 to 2.49 effective cycles per 64 bytes transferred over both boots (bracket time, best rows, files cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv and cme-bandwidth-dram-1core-asmpasses.csv [Ref11] [Ref12]).
  • A straight line through the write time per pass at 4 KiB, 8 KiB, 16 KiB and 24 KiB passes the plan rule (single-call form, span time, best rows, file cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv). Its slope is 52.1 GB/s est. on boot F1 (largest residual 1.1 % of the smallest pass time) and 52.2 GB/s est. on boot F2 (largest residual 0.8 % of the smallest pass time).

Why it is not explained

  • The buffer of 16 KiB is smaller than the CME L1 of 64 KiB. The ratio is the same with the prefetchers on (2.31) and off (2.33). So a refill is not expected.
  • The bandwidth rows carry no counters [Ref32]. So no count confirms that.
  • No row isolates the store path. The test plan records the same question and says that no row isolates the cause [Ref60].

Hypotheses

Hypothesis

The write throughput is a limit of the store path of the CME itself. The single-call write rows transfer 64 bytes every 2.38 to 2.49 effective cycles from 4 KiB to 256 KiB (bracket time, best rows, both boots).

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A CME event that counts the stores that wait for a free entry of the store buffer, read on a write row. Or the store timing in the RTL. No kernel on these boots can separate the store path from the rest of the write loop.

What would settle it

  • A counter of the store path on a write row.
  • The store timing of the CME in the RTL or in the Arm technical reference manual of the C1-SME2.

9.3 The looped write reads faster in its span than the single-call write

  • Inside the span the looped write reads up to 93.5 GB/s on boot F1 and 93.3 GB/s on boot F2, both at 8 KiB. The single-call write reads 52.3 to 54.0 GB/s in its span.
  • A span rate above the single-call rate fits a span that does not hold all the store work of its call. No row shows that mechanism, so it is a hypothesis.
  • The figure and the table of the write forms are in section 7.8. The rows of one write call are in section 7.4.

Observation

  • A looped pass minus a single-call pass reads +75.6, +6.9, -0.7, -2.0 ns at 4 KiB, 8 KiB, 16 KiB and 24 KiB on boot F1, and +73.1, +8.8, -1.4, -0.3 ns on boot F2 (bracket time per pass, files cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv [Ref43] [Ref47] and cme-bandwidth-l1-asmpasses.csv [Ref9] [Ref10]).
  • So at 16 KiB and 24 KiB a looped pass and a single-call pass take the same time within 2.0 ns, although the looped form makes one kernel call per pass.
  • Each looped write call still spends 76.1 to 91.9 ns outside its span on boot F1 and 76.2 to 79.9 ns on boot F2 (all reps of the looped write rows, 4 KiB to 24 KiB).
  • One write call of 1 KiB, 2 KiB, 4 KiB and 8 KiB spends 48.0, 52.5, 73.5, 91.6 ns in its span on boot F1 (file cme-bandwidth-call-cost.csv [Ref48]).
  • From 4 KiB to 8 KiB that is 18.1 ns for 4,096 more bytes. The apparent rate of those bytes is 226 GB/s est. The single-call write reads at most 54.0 GB/s.
  • The four looped points do not lie on one line. The largest residual is 18.4 % of the smallest pass time on boot F1 and 17.8 % on boot F2. The plan rule voids the intercept. So this page quotes no fixed cost per call for the looped write.
  • With a DSB ST before SMSTOP the pass takes 76.9 ns longer at 16 KiB and 74.3 ns longer at 24 KiB on boot F1 (file cme-bandwidth-l1-dsb.csv [Ref54] [Ref55]). That is close to the outside-span time of one call.

Why it is not explained

  • The run plan states that the span of a store call does not wait for the stores unless the kernel ends with DSB ST [Ref49]. No row of these boots shows that mechanism.
  • If the statement holds, the span time and the outside-span time each include an unknown part of the store work. These rows do not separate the two parts.
  • The run plan names no observation that would identify the mechanism [Ref49].

Hypotheses

Hypothesis

The span of a write call ends before the stores of the call have completed. The last stores finish while the call leaves streaming mode and the next call enters it. So the cost of the call overlaps with store work.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A write kernel with a third stamp after a DSB ST in the same call. It gives the store completion time of each call. The DSB ST rows of these boots are consistent with the hypothesis and do not prove it.

What would settle it

  • A kernel that stamps the time before and after a DSB ST inside one call. This is a proposal of this page, not of the run plan.

9.4 The fixed cost of a call, and the extra time of a call alone in its bracket

  • On the cme-call rows (64 calls that follow each other, one register step each) a call spends 63.5 to 64.6 ns outside its span.
  • Looped bandwidth calls spend 75.8 to 398.0 ns outside their spans.
  • One call alone in its bracket spends 286 ns on both boots (median). That is 222 ns more than a call of the cme-call rows.
  • No row separates SMSTART and SMSTOP from the register save, the restore, the call and the return. No row shows what the extra time of a lone call is.
  • The figure and the two tables of these rows are in section 7.6.

Observation

  • The outside-span time is not one number. It reads 63.5 to 64.6 ns per call on the cme-call rows, 75.8 to 106.2 ns on the looped rows from 16 KiB to 256 KiB, and 118.5 to 398.0 ns from 1 MiB to 32 MiB.
  • A call alone in its bracket spends 286 to 292 ns outside its span on boot F1 and 280 to 304 ns on boot F2 (OCM latency passes of 64 loads, 35 passes per boot).
  • The single-call read reps show the same level with no counter call before them: 280.0 to 300.9 ns for the reps after the first, on both boots (24 reps per boot). So a counter call cannot be the only cause.
  • Each of these reps follows a warm-up pass that is not timed and a thread barrier (the point where the worker thread waits for the main thread before each rep) [Ref32]. So these reps do not test whether a thread barrier before the call matters.
  • The first rep of each single-call read row spends 339.9 to 408.0 ns. That is more than every later rep.
  • The single-call write reps after the first spend a median of 383.3 ns on boot F1 and 382.2 ns on boot F2 (354.6 to 427.8 ns over both boots). That is 97 ns and 98 ns above the read reps. Section 9.3 gives a hypothesis for the store part.
  • The core cycle count of a counting window is 583 to 603 cycles above the CME cycle count of the same window (medians). The difference is the same with 1 call and with 64 calls per window. Converted to time at 2.00 core cycles per ns it is 292 to 302 ns.
  • So each added call adds about the same number of cycles to both counts, its outside-span time included.
  • Each cycle count is one total per window. The files hold no time of a counter start or stop. So they do not show at which time in the window the two counters differ.
  • The two clock reads of an empty bracket take 39.0 ns in 23 of the 24 CME latency files (40.0 ns in the other one).

Why it is not explained

  • No row separates SMSTART and SMSTOP from the register save, the restore, the call and the return.
  • Every CME kernel of these boots takes the two stamps of its span. No row runs without them. So the share of the stamps in each number is not measured.
  • The power controller of each CME is the unit that switches the CME on and off. The firmware sets it to dynamic mode (operator's README) [Ref20]. The files do not record whether the CME powers down between two spans.
  • The run plan leaves the extra time of a lone call open by choice and has no dedicated row for it [Ref49].

Hypotheses

Hypothesis

The CME leaves a low-power state at the first streaming instruction after an idle interval. The extra time of a lone call is the time to leave that state.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: Rows that vary the idle time before one call (0, 1, 10 and 100 microseconds) and read the outside-span time, with the status of the CME power controller read before and after the call.

Hypothesis

The clock of the CME, or its cycle counter, does not run from the counter start until the first streaming entry of the window. Then the extra time occurs once per window and not once per call. Under this hypothesis the 64 calls of a cme-call rep split as follows. The lowest rep spends 4,065 ns outside its spans in total on boot F1 (4,066 ns on boot F2). The first call takes the 286 ns of a lone call (a median). That leaves 60.0 ns est. for each of the 63 later calls on boot F1 and 60.0 ns est. on boot F2. No row measures a later call alone, so this arithmetic is not a test.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A time stamp before SMSTART in the kernel, or the status of the CME power controller read before and after a lone call.

Hypothesis

The core cycle counter and the CME cycle counter do not start and stop at the same instant inside the counter calls. Then the difference of 583 to 603 cycles between the two cycle counts of a window is a property of the counter calls. It says nothing about the clock of the CME.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A counting window with no kernel call in it, with both cycle counts printed. The hypothesis predicts the same difference there.

Hypothesis

The first call after a counter start, a flush or a thread barrier has cache misses and branch predictor misses in the core. The CME is not involved. The single-call read reps show that a counter start is not needed for the extra time. The longer first rep of each single-call row is consistent with a first-call cost in the core.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: One bracket that holds two calls with a controlled idle time between them and no system call. The second call shows whether the extra time needs a system call or a barrier before it. A second test: count the cache refills and the branch mispredictions of the core over a lone call and over the second of two calls. Equal counts reject this hypothesis.

What would settle it

  • The same script on one boot with a build whose stamps are compiled out.
  • Rows that vary the idle time before a single call, with the power controller status beside them.
  • A stamp before SMSTART, to split the time before the span from the time after it.

9.5 Every rep counts about one inner refill per line of the chain, also when the chain fits in the CME L1

  • On boot F2 every timed rep of a chain of 4 KiB to 64 KiB counts about one inner refill per line of the chain (0.99 to 1.02 as printed, in all 21 rep rows, file cme-latency-dram-small.csv [Ref1]).
  • Two walks that are not timed run before the first rep [Ref29].
  • The count is a total over one rep. It does not say which lines were refilled, or at which time in the rep.
  • A rep whose first walk refills every line of the chain would give this count. That reading is a hypothesis below. The cause of the refills is not measured.
  • The figure and the table of these rows are in section 4.7.

Observation

  • The count per line reads about one in every rep, although the chain was walked twice before the first rep and many times inside each rep.
  • The file prints the count per load to four decimals. One print step is 0.10 refills per line at 4 KiB and 0.006 at 64 KiB. So the count per line is not known more exactly than that.
  • The chain load is 0.010 to 0.235 ns above the round-trip baseline of 21.005 ns at these footprints.
  • The looped bandwidth rows differ for calls that follow each other. The fitted span rate of the looped read from 4 KiB to 24 KiB is 134.7 GB/s est. on boot F1 and 132.9 GB/s est. on boot F2, and both fits pass the plan rule (file cme-bandwidth-l1-passes.csv).
  • That rate is 3.1 times the 43.7 GB/s of the 96 KiB read row of boot F1, which does not fit in the CME L1. No bandwidth row has a refill counter.
  • One known difference between the two cases: a latency rep has a counter stop, a counter read and a counter start before its call [Ref29]. A looped bandwidth pass has none [Ref32].
  • The two cases also use different kernels. Only the latency run has the CME counters enabled.

Why it is not explained

  • Each rep row holds one refill total for the whole rep. No row counts the first walk of a rep apart from the later walks.
  • No row records the address of a refilled line. So the rows do not show whether each line of the chain is refilled one time, or which state the CME L1 has at the start of a rep.
  • No latency row ran without the counters, and no rep loop ran without a counter call between the reps.

Hypotheses

Hypothesis

Each rep starts with a CME L1 that does not hold the chain. The first walk of the rep refills every line of the chain one time. The later walks of the rep refill no line.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A rep that counts its first walk apart from its later walks. The hypothesis predicts one inner refill per line in the first walk and none in the later walks. A trace of the refilled addresses would show the history of each line.

Hypothesis

The difference between the chain load and the round-trip baseline at 4 KiB to 64 KiB comes from these refills. It is not the cost of a load that hits the CME L1. Support: that difference divided by the refill count is 10 to 15 ns est. per refill, close to the 11.8 to 15.2 ns est. per refill of the rows from 96 KiB to 384 KiB. The value at 4 KiB has one significant digit, because the count per load prints as 0.0010.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A latency run without the counter option, or a rep loop with no system call between the reps. The hypothesis predicts a lower chain load at these footprints when the refills are absent.

Hypothesis

The CME loses the content of its L1 when the core runs a system call between two spans, for example because the CME powers down (see section 9.4).

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: The same latency rows with a varied idle time and with the number of system calls between the reps set to zero, one and two.

Hypothesis

In the looped bandwidth rows from 4 KiB to 24 KiB the lines of the buffer stay in the CME L1 from one call to the next.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: The CME refill counters on the looped bandwidth rows. The hypothesis predicts a count near zero refills per line in a call that follows another call.

What would settle it

  • A rep that counts its first walk and its later walks apart, to show at which time the refills occur.
  • A trace of the refilled addresses, to show the history of each line.
  • A latency sweep from 4 KiB to 64 KiB without the counter option.
  • A rep loop with no system call between the reps, with the counters read once around all reps.

9.6 What the L3 events count

  • The three L3 events of the CME are exploratory counts. No row on these boots is built so that every L3 access is a hit, or every one a miss.
  • On boot F2 the hit count rises from 0.14 per load at 96 KiB to 0.64 at 384 KiB while the chain load falls from 35.996 ns to 32.910 ns. That agrees with a real hit count and does not validate it.
  • The figure and the table of these rows are in section 5.3 (files cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv [Ref38] [Ref45] and cme-latency-dram-large-l3.csv [Ref39] [Ref46]).

Table 62. Miss minus refill per load times the footprint, per rep, boot F2, walked many times. The value is a derived product in KiB: (L3 miss count per load minus L3 refill count per load) x footprint (file cme-latency-dram-small-l3.csv [Ref38]).

FootprintRep 0, KiBRep 1, KiBRep 2, KiBChain load, first to last rep, nsL3 hit count per load, first to last rep
96 KiB82.883.381.236.195 to 35.9960.1261 to 0.1415
128 KiB110.6103.298.236.256 to 35.5240.1357 to 0.2329
192 KiB120.8100.797.234.592 to 33.6610.3700 to 0.4934
256 KiB121.499.396.733.778 to 32.7880.5032 to 0.6186
384 KiB123.299.396.532.910 to 33.4370.6375 to 0.6318

The product is built from event totals per load. It does not identify a set of lines of the chain. The three events are exploratory, so the product is an exploratory value too.

Observation

  • From 96 KiB to 256 KiB the chain load falls as the footprint grows, and the L3 hit count per load rises (section 4.3, section 5.2).
  • In the last rep the derived product, miss minus refill times the footprint, reads 96.5 to 98.2 KiB at every footprint from 128 KiB to 384 KiB. At 96 KiB it reads 81.2 KiB.
  • At each of these 4 footprints the product falls from rep to rep.
  • So the derived product is nearly the same at these 4 footprints. The product comes from event totals per load. It does not show whether the same lines of the chain count as "L3 miss, no L3 refill" in every walk.
  • The core writes the buffer and the chain pointers before the CME walks them (section 2.3). The L1 data cache and the L2 of CPU 2 hold 160 KiB together [Ref15].
  • The L3 refill count equals the outer refill count to the four printed decimals in all 58 chain rep rows of each boot.
  • Hit plus miss equals inner refills plus outer refills within 0.0001 per load in every row of both boots.
  • From 4 KiB to 64 KiB on boot F2 all three events read at most 0.013 per load (best reps).
  • On boot F1 hit plus miss reads up to 16.64 per load (best reps). It is above one per load from 8 KiB to 32 MiB. The plain rows of boot F1 count up to 15.89 prefetch refills per load.

Why it is not explained

  • The events have no independent control. No boot whose L3 holds no data ran them through the CME. So "the hit count reads 0 when the L3 is empty" is not checked.
  • One reading is: hit = refills that the L3 supplied, miss minus refill = refills that a snoop of a core's cache supplied. It comes from the operator's reading of the RTL [Ref21]. Under that reading the two equalities above are identities. They validate nothing.
  • The test program itself marks the three columns as exploratory [Ref33].

Hypotheses

Hypothesis

The hit event counts the CME L1 refills that the cluster L3 supplied. Miss minus refill counts the refills that a snoop of a core's cache supplied. The refill event counts the lines that came from outside the cluster.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: The two L3-event sweeps on a boot whose L3 holds no data: the hit count must read 0 there. And one row built so that every refill comes from the L3: the hit count must read 1 per load there.

Hypothesis

The derived product stands for a fixed set of lines. A part of the chain of 96.5 to 98.2 KiB stays in the caches of CPU 2, the core that wrote the buffer. A CME refill that a snoop of a core's cache supplies (operator's README) does not move the line to the cluster L3. So the same lines are snooped again in every walk. The rest of the chain is in the L3, and its share grows with the footprint. A snoop takes longer than an L3 hit. So the chain load falls as the footprint grows.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: Let the CME write the buffer and the chain pointers. Or let the core walk another buffer of 160 KiB or more before the reps. The hypothesis predicts a miss minus refill near 0 per load after either step, and a chain load that does not fall as the footprint grows.

What would settle it

  • The two sweeps with the L3 events on a boot with the L3 in its mode that holds no data.
  • A row whose refills all come from one source.
  • The rows of 96 KiB to 384 KiB after the CME wrote the buffer, or after the core walked another buffer of 160 KiB or more.
  • The run plan names both controls and schedules neither [Ref49].
Note

Until a control validates these events, no result on this page depends on the hit column or on the miss column. A fit that uses them appears only inside a Hypothesis block.

9.7 The chain load on boot F1 falls between 384 KiB and 512 KiB

  • On boot F1 the chain load falls by 10.594 ns from 384 KiB to 512 KiB. On boot F2 it rises by 4.677 ns. For the core on boot F1 it rises by 6.478 ns.
  • The chain kind changes at the same place: "walked many times" stops at 384 KiB and "walked once" starts at 512 KiB. So the fall cannot be assigned to the footprint or to the chain kind.
  • The figure and the table of the step are in section 4.5 (files cme-latency-dram-small.csv [Ref1] [Ref5] and cme-latency-dram-large.csv [Ref3] [Ref6]).

Observation

  • On boot F1 the CME counts 14.36 prefetch refills per load at 384 KiB and 5.36 at 512 KiB.
  • Boot F2 and the core on boot F1 both rise at the same place.

Why it is not explained

  • The two files differ in the footprint and in the chain kind at once.

Hypotheses

Hypothesis

The chain kind causes the fall. A chain walked many times gives the prefetcher of the CME the same lines again and again, and its refills displace lines of the chain. A chain walked once does not.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: The footprints 384 KiB and 512 KiB, each run with both chain kinds, on a boot with the prefetchers on. If the fall follows the kind and not the footprint, the hypothesis is confirmed.

What would settle it

Insufficient data

No footprint has both chain kinds. One footprint between 384 KiB and 512 KiB that is walked many times and walked once, on both boots, would assign the step to the footprint or to the chain kind.

9.8 Differences between boot F1 and boot F2 whose mechanism is not measured

  • With the prefetchers on, a chain that fits in the CME L1 reads up to 24.3 ns slower per load (64 KiB). The 8 MiB chain with every line flushed first reads 9.6 ns faster.
  • The two boots differ in more than the prefetcher setting. So a difference between them is not by itself an effect of the prefetchers.
  • The figure and the table of the chain loads of both boots are in section 4.4 (files cme-latency-dram-small.csv, cme-latency-dram-large.csv and cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv [Ref2] [Ref8]). The bandwidth rows are drawn below.

Observation

  • On boot F1 the CME counts 4.0 to 15.9 prefetch refills per load on chains of 8 KiB to 64 KiB, which fit in its L1 of 64 KiB.
  • The 8 MiB chain with every line flushed first counts 3.41 outer refills per load on boot F1 and 1.00 on boot F2. Its read refills are 0.99 per load on boot F1.
  • So that row of boot F1 still counts about one read refill per load. Its chain load is 9.634 ns below the row of boot F2.
  • The single-call read at 96 KiB reads 68.2 GB/s on boot F1 and 42.8 GB/s on boot F2 (boot F2 is 0.63 times boot F1). Its neighbours at 48 KiB and 160 KiB agree between the boots within 1.0 %.
  • The looped read at 32 MiB reads 36.6 GB/s on boot F1 and 17.7 GB/s on boot F2 (boot F2 is 0.48 times boot F1). The write at 32 MiB differs by 0.2 %.

Why it is not explained

  • The firmware of boot F2 turns off the prefetcher of the core and the prefetcher of the CME together (operator's README) [Ref21]. So the rows do not show which of the two causes a difference.
  • The boots differ in what ran before the CME rows. The first CME command starts 1.87 s after boot on boot F1, after 67 core commands, and 0.34 s after boot on boot F2, which ran no core command [Ref22] [Ref23].
  • Each command is its own process on each boot. So its buffers need not be on the same physical pages (operator's README) [Ref21].
  • The refill events count lines. They do not show which lines a prefetch refill replaced, or which prefetched lines the walk used.
  • No boot was repeated. So the spread between two boots with the same settings is not known.

Hypotheses

Hypothesis

On a chain that fits in the CME L1, the refills of the prefetcher evict lines of the chain. Those lines then refill on demand.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A count of CME L1 evictions, or a trace of one walk. The read refills of 0.17 to 0.85 per load on boot F1 are consistent with it.

Hypothesis

The prefetch refills occupy the refill path of the CME, and loads that hit the CME L1 wait behind them.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: The same chains on a boot with only the prefetcher of the CME on. The hypothesis predicts the same rise with the prefetcher of the core off. The RTL of the refill path would show whether a load that hits the CME L1 can wait behind a refill.

Hypothesis

On the 8 MiB chain with every line flushed first, the prefetcher requests the lines next to each loaded line. The chain covers every line. So a load finds its line already requested, and its read refill completes sooner.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: A chain of 8 MiB with one line per 4 KiB page, walked once, on both boots: no neighbouring line is ever loaded there. And a chain in address order (see section 9.12).

Hypothesis

At 96 KiB in the single-call form, with all passes in one span, the prefetcher fetches each line before the read reaches it, at this one footprint.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: Single-call read rows at footprints between 48 KiB and 160 KiB, and CME counters on a bandwidth row.

What would settle it

  • A boot with only the prefetcher of the CME off and the prefetcher of the core on.
  • A boot that runs the commands of boot F1 in the same order with the prefetchers off.
  • A second boot with the settings of boot F1, for the spread between boots.

9.9 Which level outside the cluster serves a load

  • On boot F2 the chain load rises from 43.666 ns at 3 MiB to 71.068 ns at 32 MiB. The outer refill count stays at 0.93 to 1.00 per load over these rows.
  • The outer refill event counts every refill from outside the cluster. It does not separate the SLC from the DRAM model.
  • The figure of these rows is in section 4.1 and their table in section 4.8 (chains walked once, file cme-latency-dram-large.csv).

Observation

  • The boot F2 line is flat from 1 MiB to 3 MiB (42.125 ns to 43.666 ns) and reads 47.328 ns at 4 MiB.
  • From 3 MiB to 8 MiB it rises by 19.2 ns.
  • The SLC holds 5 MiB x 12/16 = 3.75 MiB est. after the OCM ways are taken out (operator's README) [Ref20]. That size lies between 3 MiB and 4 MiB.
  • The 8 MiB chain with every line flushed first reads 71.714 ns on boot F2, 50.709 ns above the round-trip baseline (file cme-latency-dram-flushed.csv).

Why it is not explained

  • The mesh counters cover a whole command: the chain build, the flushes and the untimed walks are included. They exist for 15 CME commands per boot, and no footprint sweep is among them [Ref22] [Ref23].
  • The memory behind the home nodes is an emulator model with no configured delay (operator's README) [Ref20]. So the highest level of these rows is the delay of the RTL stages on the path plus that model. It is not the timing of silicon DRAM.

Hypotheses

Hypothesis

The rise between 3 MiB and 8 MiB is the chain growing beyond the SLC of 3.75 MiB est.

Measurement that would confirm or reject it: Mesh counts restricted to the timed pass of each footprint, or an SLC hit event per load. The hypothesis predicts that the share of loads the SLC serves falls from 4 MiB up.

What would settle it

  • Mesh counts per footprint that cover only the timed pass.
  • A run with a DRAM-like delay profile on the memory model, or silicon, for the level above the SLC.

Hypothesis

The OCM regions differ because of the distance on the mesh. The home nodes of regions 3 and 4 are 2 steps further from the cluster of CPU 2 than those of regions 0 to 2. The position of that cluster on the mesh is itself a hypothesis.

9.11 Not measured on these boots

  • Every CME row of both boots runs one thread on CPU 2: 70 of 70 CME commands on boot F1 and 70 of 70 on boot F2 name CPU 2 [Ref22] [Ref23].
  • The other core of the cluster is offline for the whole CME script [Ref22] [Ref23] [Ref24].
  • So these boots measure one CME, used by one core. Every latency row returns its value to the core.
  • The diagram shows what lies outside that.

The CME itself
What the round-trip baseline is made ofThe baseline is 21.005 ns in all 24 CME latency files (best rows). It reads 42.01 core cycles per step in 68 of the 72 rep rows and 42.02 in the other 4. It is a separate measurement of a kernel with no memory access: a register copy takes the place of the load. No row splits it into the issue to the CME, the execution and the return. Every chain load also returns its value to the core through LASTB. No row calibrates the non-memory cost that the chain kernel and the baseline kernel share. So the chain load minus the baseline is a difference between two kernels. It is not identified as memory-access time.A waveform of one DUP+LASTB step from the RTL, or the interface timing in the Arm technical reference manual of the C1-SME2. A calibration of the non-memory cost that the two kernels share.
A load-to-use time that stays in the vector registersEvery latency row returns the value to the core through LASTB.A kernel with a dependent load chain inside the CME.
Access kinds that no kernel runsLoads and stores of the ZA array, gather loads, vectors that are not aligned to 64 bytes or that cross a page, loads with a partial predicate (other than the 8-byte chain load), a store followed by a load of the same line.New kernels in cme_kern.S.
Copy rows beyond the looped sweepThe copy kernel exists only in the looped sweep (looped form, 16 KiB to 32 MiB). No single-call copy and no copy on the OCM exist.Copy rows in the single-call form, below 16 KiB, and on the OCM.
A write rate with a known destination levelThe OCM write (30.7 GB/s on boot F1, 31.0 GB/s on boot F2) is the only write row under the mesh counters. The destination of no other write row is known.CME counters on a bandwidth row, and write rows under the mesh counters.
CME bandwidth rows with countersThe bandwidth program refuses its counter option together with the CME option [Ref32].A CME counter set in the bandwidth program.
Sharing
Two cores of one cluster in streaming mode at onceCPU 3 is offline in every CME command. The program takes one worker with the CME option, because the two stamps of a span are one global pair [Ref32].A CME read and write on CPUs 2 and 3 together. The program needs stamps per thread first.
More than one CME at onceNo row runs the CMEs of two clusters together, and no CME row runs on a CPU other than CPU 2 [Ref60]. So the aggregate CME bandwidth and the behaviour of the other CMEs are not known.The same script pinned to a core of another cluster, and one run with several clusters at once.
Conditions
A repeat of a bootBoots that were repeated: 0. Inside one boot the round-trip baseline reads 21.005 ns in all 24 files.A second boot with the settings of boot F1 and one with the settings of boot F2.
The core with the prefetchers off and the L3 onBoot F2 ran 0 core commands. So the core rows beside the CME exist on boot F1 only.The core script on a boot with the firmware of boot F2.
CME rows with the cluster L3 offBoth boots have the L3 on.The CME script on a boot with the L3 in its mode that holds no data.
OCM against DRAM bandwidth under the same conditionsAn OCM read row is 1 pass after a flush. Every row of the sweep on the DRAM model runs 2 to 256 passes after a warm-up pass, with no flush.Rows on the DRAM model with a flush before one pass, at 256 KiB and at 1,280 KiB.
The cost of address translationThe CME rows carry no TLB counter. The OCM rows use 4 KiB pages and the rows on the DRAM model use 2 MiB pages. The two OCM chain shapes agree within 0.212 ns in the span on boot F2 (45.744 ns and 45.532 ns). Both walk the pages in random order, so this does not bound the cost. The chain of one line per 4 KiB page touches 320 pages, more than the 24 entries of the TLB of the CME (operator's README) [Ref20].The same OCM rows on a mapping of 64 KiB or 2 MiB pages, with the prefetchers off and the L3 on.
Chip time against siliconAll times are chip time at a measured 2.00 core cycles per ns. No file says whether the clock of the silicon target is 2 GHz.The clock specification of the design.
A chain in address orderNo row. One row of a third boot is shown in section 9.12.The address-order command on both boots.
Insufficient data

Each line of the table above is a measurement that these boots do not hold. The right column names the row that would supply it.

9.12 A chain in address order: one row from a third boot

  • Boot F1 and boot F2 have no chain in address order. In that chain kind each line holds the address of the next line of the buffer.
  • A third boot with the L3 on and the prefetchers on has one such row: 21.417 ns per load at 8 MiB with every line flushed first, 0.413 ns above the round-trip baseline of the same file [Ref61].

Table 67. Conditions and counters of the address-order row (file cme-latency-dram-seq.csv of the third boot [Ref61]).

Condition of the address-order rowValueSource
Cluster L3on (the operator's README calls it full mode)operator's README [Ref62]
Hardware prefetchersonoperator's README [Ref62]
OCM translations4 KiBoperator's README [Ref62]
Program buildanother commit than boot F1 and boot F2, with no span columnoperator's README [Ref62]
CPU and memoryCPU 2, DRAM, huge pages (backing=hugetlb in the file)file header
Chain8 MiB, 131,072 lines, address order (seq=1), every line flushed first (flush=1), walked once per repfile header
Best chain load21.417 nsfile, best row
Round-trip baseline of the same file21.004 nsfile
Prefetch refills per load1.0000file, best rep
Outer refills per load1.0000file, best rep
Read refills per load2.289e-05 as printedfile, best rep
Loads per timed pass131,072file, each rep row
Read refills per timed pass3 in each of the 2 timed passes (count per load x loads, rounded to a whole event)computed from the file
  • The row counts 1.00 prefetch refill and 1.00 outer refill per load.
  • It also counts 3 read refills in each of its 2 timed passes of 131,072 loads. The file prints 2.289e-05 read refills per load, and that count times the loads gives 3.
  • So the refills are almost all attributed to the prefetcher. The counts are totals of a pass. They do not show that the prefetcher requested every line of the chain.
  • The row comes from another boot and another program build. It shows the case and does not belong to the results of boot F1 or boot F2.
Insufficient data

No address-order chain exists with the L3 on and the prefetchers off. The address-order command on boot F2 would give the value with no prefetched lines.

9.13 Statements the data do not support

  • Each statement below is close to a number on this page. The rows of boot F1 and boot F2 do not support it. The right column says what the rows do show.
  • The statements about fits and about the write rate are in section 3.5. The statements about the cost of a call are in section 7.9. They are not repeated here.

Table 68. Statements that the rows of boot F1 and boot F2 do not support.

StatementWhat the rows show
"An L3-served CME load takes 32.8 ns."The 256 KiB row of boot F2 reads that. The exploratory hit event counts only 0.50 to 0.62 L3 hits per load at that footprint, and the event is not validated.
"The L3 supplies X % of the refills of the CME."The split into hits and misses depends on a reading of the RTL with no control row.
"The prefetcher causes every difference between boot F1 and boot F2."The boots also differ in what ran before the CME rows and in the placement of each buffer. No boot was repeated.
"The prefetcher of the CME helps" or "hurts", as a general ruleWith the prefetchers on the chain load is higher on all 12 chains walked many times (4 KiB to 384 KiB) and on the chains walked once from 512 KiB to 8 MiB. It is lower on the chains walked once at 16 MiB and 32 MiB and on the 8 MiB chain with every line flushed first. The looped read rate at 32 MiB is 2.1 times higher with the prefetchers on.
"The OCM costs 37 ns through the CME."That is the bracket time of one region on boot F1 (32.8 ns in the span). The one-region rows of boot F1 count 0.22 to 0.58 prefetch refills per load. With the prefetchers off (boot F2) the regions read 43.453 to 47.734 ns in the span.
"Two cores that share a CME each get half", or any sum over several CMEsNo such row exists.
"The outer refills are DRAM reads."Outer means outside the cluster: the SLC, the OCM or the DRAM model.
"The span rate is the rate of the memory path."Every bandwidth number is the rate of a whole kernel: loads, XOR instructions and loop instructions are included.
"A refill count of 0.5 per load means that half the loads missed."The refill events count lines that enter the CME L1. They do not say which load waited for which line.
"A 64-byte load takes 1.06 cycles" or "a 64-byte store takes 2.45 cycles."Those values are effective cycles per 64 bytes transferred: 64 bytes divided by the throughput of a whole loop (16 KiB, single-call form, span time, boot F1). Each load or store instruction of the loop transfers four 64-byte vectors, and the read loop also runs XOR instructions. No row times one load or one store (section 9.2).
"A chain load is the round-trip baseline plus the time of the memory access."The round-trip baseline (21.005 ns) is a separate measurement of a kernel with no memory access. The chain load minus the baseline is a difference between two kernels. No row calibrates the non-memory cost that the two kernels share. So the difference is not identified as memory-access time.
"Each rep refills every line of the chain one time."The rep rows of boot F2 count about one inner refill per line of the chain (0.99 to 1.02 as printed, 4 KiB to 64 KiB). That is a total over one rep. It does not say which lines were refilled, or at which time in the rep (section 9.5).
"Every other CME behaves like this one."Only the CME of the cluster of CPU 2 is measured.
